find_project_root <- function() {
  input_file <- tryCatch(
    knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE),
    error = function(e) ""
  )
  if (
    length(input_file) == 0L ||
      is.na(input_file[[1]]) ||
      !nzchar(input_file[[1]])
  ) {
    input_file <- ""
  } else {
    input_file <- input_file[[1]]
  }
  input_dir <- if (nzchar(input_file)) dirname(input_file) else character()
  configured_root <- Sys.getenv("EQUITY_BROCHURE_ROOT", unset = "")
  candidates <- unique(c(
    getwd(),
    input_dir,
    if (length(input_dir)) dirname(input_dir) else character(),
    configured_root,
    file.path(
      USERPROFILE,
      "Dropbox/UNICEF Work/IGME report etc/2025/Equity brochure"
    )
  ))
  candidates <- candidates[nzchar(candidates)]
  marker <- "output/aggregate/aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"
  found <- candidates[file.exists(file.path(candidates, marker))]
  if (!length(found)) {
    stop(
      "Could not locate the Equity brochure project root. ",
      "Render from the project folder or update find_project_root()."
    )
  }
  normalizePath(found[[1]], winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
}

html_escape <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  unicode_fallbacks <- c(
    "2013" = "-",
    "201C" = "\"",
    "201D" = "\"",
    "2212" = "-",
    "2265" = ">="
  )
  for (code in names(unicode_fallbacks)) {
    x <- gsub(
      intToUtf8(strtoi(code, base = 16L)),
      unicode_fallbacks[[code]],
      x,
      fixed = TRUE
    )
    x <- gsub(
      paste0("<U+", code, ">"),
      unicode_fallbacks[[code]],
      x,
      fixed = TRUE
    )
  }
  x <- gsub("&", "&amp;", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("<", "&lt;", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub(">", "&gt;", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x
}

style_value <- function(value, status) {
  css_class <- switch(
    status,
    match = "value-match",
    mismatch = "value-mismatch",
    unavailable = "value-unavailable",
    stop("Unknown status: ", status)
  )
  sprintf(
    "<span class=\"%s\">%s</span>",
    css_class,
    html_escape(value)
  )
}

format_num <- function(x, digits = 1, big_mark = ",") {
  formatC(
    x,
    format = "f",
    digits = digits,
    big.mark = big_mark
  )
}

format_int <- function(x) {
  formatC(round(x), format = "d", big.mark = ",")
}

make_result <- function(
  page,
  item,
  brochure,
  recalculated,
  status,
  action,
  source
) {
  data.frame(
    Page = as.character(page),
    Item = item,
    `Brochure value or wording` = style_value(brochure, status),
    `Recalculated / reviewed result` = style_value(recalculated, status),
    Status = style_value(
      switch(
        status,
        match = "MATCH",
        mismatch = "CORRECTION",
        unavailable = "NOT RECALCULATED"
      ),
      status
    ),
    `Recommended action` = action,
    Source = source,
    check.names = FALSE,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

mask_user_profile <- function(path) {
  normalized <- normalizePath(path, winslash = "/", mustWork = TRUE)
  if (startsWith(tolower(normalized), tolower(USERPROFILE))) {
    paste0(
      "%USERPROFILE%",
      substring(normalized, nchar(USERPROFILE) + 1L)
    )
  } else {
    normalized
  }
}

weighted_rate <- function(
  equity,
  indicator,
  group,
  type = NULL,
  year = 2024.5
) {
  x <- aggregate[
    aggregate$equity == equity &
      aggregate$Indicator == indicator &
      as.character(aggregate$Group) == as.character(group) &
      aggregate$Year == year,
  ]
  if (!is.null(type)) {
    x <- x[x$type == type, ]
  }
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) {
    stop(
      "Expected one aggregate row for ",
      paste(equity, indicator, group, type, sep = " / "),
      "; found ",
      nrow(x)
    )
  }
  x$wgt.rate[[1]]
}

country_ratios <- function(
  data,
  label,
  indicator,
  numerator,
  denominator
) {
  x <- data[
    data$label == label &
      data$Indicator == indicator &
      data$Group %in% c(numerator, denominator),
    c("Country.Code", "Country.Name", "Group", "Estimates")
  ]
  numerator_rows <- x[x$Group == numerator, c("Country.Code", "Country.Name", "Estimates")]
  denominator_rows <- x[x$Group == denominator, c("Country.Code", "Estimates")]
  names(numerator_rows)[names(numerator_rows) == "Estimates"] <- "numerator"
  names(denominator_rows)[names(denominator_rows) == "Estimates"] <- "denominator"
  out <- merge(numerator_rows, denominator_rows, by = "Country.Code")
  if (anyDuplicated(out$Country.Code)) {
    stop("Duplicate country rows in ratio calculation: ", label, " / ", indicator)
  }
  out$ratio <- out$numerator / out$denominator
  out
}

annual_reduction_rate <- function(start_value, end_value, years) {
  100 * log(start_value / end_value) / years
}

world_country_death_totals <- function(year) {
  world_country_year <- country_results[
    country_results$Sex == "Total" &
      country_results$Year == year &
      country_results$Shortind %in% c(
        "Under.five.deaths",
        "Neonatal.deaths"
      ),
  ]
  u5_rows <- world_country_year[
    world_country_year$Shortind == "Under.five.deaths",
  ]
  nmr_rows <- world_country_year[
    world_country_year$Shortind == "Neonatal.deaths",
  ]
  if (
    length(unique(u5_rows$ISO.Code)) != 200L ||
      length(unique(nmr_rows$ISO.Code)) != 200L ||
      anyDuplicated(u5_rows$ISO.Code) ||
      anyDuplicated(nmr_rows$ISO.Code)
  ) {
    stop(
      "Expected exactly one under-five-deaths row and one neonatal-deaths ",
      "row for each of the 200 countries in ", year, "."
    )
  }
  u5 <- sum(u5_rows$Median, na.rm = TRUE)
  nmr <- sum(nmr_rows$Median, na.rm = TRUE)
  list(u5 = u5, nmr = nmr, mr1t59 = u5 - nmr)
}

snapshot_specs <- data.frame(
  Determinant = c(
    "Wealth: poorest / wealthiest",
    "Education: no/primary / secondary+",
    "Residence: rural / urban",
    "Mother's age: under 20 / 20-29",
    "Mother's age: 40-49 / 20-29",
    "Birth interval: under 2 years / 3 years",
    "Birth order: fourth+ / second-third",
    "Birth size: small/very small / average/large"
  ),
  Equity = c(
    "Wealth quintile",
    "Mother's education",
    "Residence",
    "Mother's age",
    "Mother's age",
    "Birth interval",
    "Birth order",
    "Birth size"
  ),
  Numerator = c(
    "1.quintile",
    "noedu.primary",
    "rural",
    "<20",
    "40-49",
    "<2",
    "4+",
    "small.vsmall"
  ),
  Denominator = c(
    "5.quintile",
    "sec.higher",
    "urban",
    "20-29",
    "20-29",
    "3",
    "2-3",
    "av.large"
  ),
  Type = c(
    NA,
    "combined all countries",
    rep(NA, 6)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

snapshot_indicators <- c("U5MR", "NMR", "MR1t59")
snapshot_rows <- list()
row_index <- 1L

for (i in seq_len(nrow(snapshot_specs))) {
  for (indicator in snapshot_indicators) {
    # The designed birth-size snapshot reports only NMR.
    if (snapshot_specs$Determinant[[i]] == "Birth size: small/very small / average/large" &&
        indicator != "NMR") {
      next
    }
    type <- snapshot_specs$Type[[i]]
    if (is.na(type)) {
      type <- NULL
    }
    numerator_rate <- weighted_rate(
      snapshot_specs$Equity[[i]],
      indicator,
      snapshot_specs$Numerator[[i]],
      type
    )
    denominator_rate <- weighted_rate(
      snapshot_specs$Equity[[i]],
      indicator,
      snapshot_specs$Denominator[[i]],
      type
    )
    ratio <- numerator_rate / denominator_rate
    snapshot_rows[[row_index]] <- data.frame(
      Determinant = snapshot_specs$Determinant[[i]],
      Indicator = indicator,
      `Exact recalculated ratio` = style_value(format_num(ratio, 3), "match"),
      `One-decimal display` = style_value(paste0(format_num(ratio, 1), "x"), "match"),
      Status = style_value("MATCH", "match"),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
    row_index <- row_index + 1L
  }
}

print_audit_table(bind_rows(snapshot_rows))

parse_ci <- function(x) {
  pieces <- strsplit(as.character(x), ";", fixed = TRUE)
  lower <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(trimws(vapply(
    pieces,
    function(y) if (length(y) >= 1) y[[1]] else NA_character_,
    character(1)
  ))))
  upper <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(trimws(vapply(
    pieces,
    function(y) if (length(y) >= 2) y[[2]] else NA_character_,
    character(1)
  ))))
  data.frame(lower = lower, upper = upper)
}

# Country-level summary of pairwise ethnic-group comparisons with the reference
# group. A significant comparison has a reported 95% ratio CI excluding 1.
# These are not omnibus tests of ethnicity and do not apply a multiplicity correction.
ethnicity_significance_summary <- function(data) {
  raw <- parse_ci(data$`95% CI`)
  adjusted <- parse_ci(data$`Adj.95% CI`)
  raw_valid <- is.finite(raw$lower) & is.finite(raw$upper)
  adjusted_valid <- is.finite(adjusted$lower) & is.finite(adjusted$upper)
  if (any(!raw_valid & data$`u5mr ratio` != 1) ||
      any(!adjusted_valid & data$`Adj.U5MR ratio` != 1)) {
    stop("Missing non-reference confidence interval in ethnicity comparison.")
  }
  data$unadjusted_significant <- raw_valid & (raw$lower > 1 | raw$upper < 1)
  data$adjusted_significant <- adjusted_valid & (adjusted$lower > 1 | adjusted$upper < 1)
  data$valid_comparison <- raw_valid & adjusted_valid
  answer <- aggregate(
    cbind(unadjusted_significant, adjusted_significant, valid_comparison) ~ ISO3Code,
    data = data, FUN = any
  )
  if (!all(answer$valid_comparison) ||
      !setequal(answer$ISO3Code, unique(data$ISO3Code))) {
    stop("Every ethnicity country must have an evaluable non-reference comparison.")
  }
  answer$lost_significance <- answer$unadjusted_significant & !answer$adjusted_significant
  answer$neither_significant <- !answer$unadjusted_significant & !answer$adjusted_significant
  answer
}
ethnicity_country_significance <- ethnicity_significance_summary(ethnicity)
countries_without_adjusted_significance <- sum(!ethnicity_country_significance$adjusted_significant)
countries_with_adjusted_significance <- sum(ethnicity_country_significance$adjusted_significant)
countries_losing_ethnicity_significance <- sum(ethnicity_country_significance$lost_significance)
countries_without_either_ethnicity_significance <- sum(ethnicity_country_significance$neither_significant)
stopifnot(countries_without_adjusted_significance ==
  countries_losing_ethnicity_significance + countries_without_either_ethnicity_significance)

# Page 36, Map 4: distinct groups in the supplied analysis dataset.
# Count the group labels themselves rather than copying the repeated gr metadata.
ethnicity_group_summary <- function(data) {
  keys <- data.frame(ISO3Code = trimws(as.character(data$ISO3Code)),
                     ethnicity = trimws(as.character(data$ethnicity)))
  if (anyNA(keys) || any(!nzchar(keys$ISO3Code)) || any(!nzchar(keys$ethnicity))) {
    stop("Missing country or ethnic-group label in ethnicity dataset.")
  }
  counts <- aggregate(ethnicity ~ ISO3Code, unique(keys), length)
  names(counts)[names(counts) == "ethnicity"] <- "groups"
  counts[order(counts$ISO3Code), ]
}

ethnicity_extreme_country_names <- function(count) {
  countries <- sort(ethnicity_group_counts$Country[ethnicity_group_counts$groups == count])
  if (length(countries) == 1L) return(countries)
  paste(paste(head(countries, -1L), collapse = ", "), tail(countries, 1L), sep = " and ")
}

external_value <- function(key) {

    external_verified_claims$key == key
  ]
  if (length(value) != 1L || is.na(value)) {
    stop("Expected one external verified value for key: ", key)

coverage_from_codes <- function(codes, year = 2024.5) {
  codes <- unique(na.omit(codes))
  country_year <- country_results[
    country_results$ISO.Code %in% codes &
      country_results$Sex == "Total" &
      country_results$Year == year,
  ]
  u5_deaths <- sum(
    country_year$Median[
      country_year$Shortind == "Under.five.deaths"
    ],
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  nmr_deaths <- sum(
    country_year$Median[
      country_year$Shortind == "Neonatal.deaths"
    ],
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  mr1t59_deaths <- u5_deaths - nmr_deaths
  world_totals <- world_country_death_totals(year)
  un_codes <- country_info$UNCode[
    country_info$ISO3Code %in% codes
  ]
  births <- sum(
    live_births$lb[
      live_births$year == year &
        live_births$sex == "b" &
        live_births$uncode %in% un_codes
    ],
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  world_country_codes <- unique(country_results$ISO.Code[
    country_results$Sex == "Total" &
      country_results$Year == year &
      country_results$Shortind == "Under.five.deaths"
  ])
  if (length(world_country_codes) != 200L) {
    stop("Expected 200 countries in the world birth denominator for ", year)
  }
  world_un_codes <- unique(country_info$UNCode[
    country_info$ISO3Code %in% world_country_codes
  ])
  if (length(world_un_codes) != 200L || anyNA(world_un_codes)) {
    stop("Expected one live-birth UN code for each of the 200 countries.")
  }
  world_births <- sum(
    live_births$lb[
      live_births$year == year &
        live_births$sex == "b" &
        live_births$uncode %in% world_un_codes
    ],
    na.rm = TRUE
  )
  list(
    countries = length(codes),
    u5_deaths = u5_deaths,
    u5_percent = 100 * u5_deaths / world_totals$u5,
    nmr_deaths = nmr_deaths,
    nmr_percent = 100 * nmr_deaths / world_totals$nmr,
    mr1t59_deaths = mr1t59_deaths,
    mr1t59_percent = 100 * mr1t59_deaths / world_totals$mr1t59,
    births = births,
    birth_percent = 100 * births / world_births
  )
}

aggregate_dimension_codes <- function(label, indicator = "U5MR") {
  codes <- unique(aggregate_country$Country.Code[
    aggregate_country$label == label &
      aggregate_country$Indicator == indicator &
      aggregate_country$Group != "total" &
      !is.na(aggregate_country$wgt.rate) &
      !is.na(aggregate_country$wgt.death)
  ])
  expected_count <- aggregate_country_count$n_countries[
    aggregate_country_count$label == label &
      aggregate_country_count$Indicator == indicator
  ]
  if (
    length(expected_count) != 1L ||
      is.na(expected_count) ||
      length(codes) != expected_count
  ) {
    stop(
      "Aggregate contributor set does not match the country-count file for ",
      label, " / ", indicator, "."
    )
  }
  codes
}

trend_summary_value <- function(label, indicator, group, field) {
  value <- trend_summary[
    trend_summary$label == label &
      trend_summary$Indicator == indicator &
      trend_summary$Group == group,
    field
  ]
  if (length(value) != 1L || is.na(value)) {
    stop(
      "Expected one trend-summary value: ",
      paste(label, indicator, group, field, sep = " / ")
    )
  }
  value
}
trend_country_codes <- function(data, label, indicator = "U5MR") {
  x <- data[data$label == label & data$Indicator == indicator &
    data$Group != "total", ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) > 0L, !anyNA(x$Country.Code),
    all(is.finite(x$wgt.rate)), all(is.finite(x$wgt.death)),
    !anyDuplicated(x[c("Country.Code", "Reference.Date", "Group")]))
  sets <- split(x$Country.Code, interaction(x$Reference.Date, x$Group, drop = TRUE))
  codes <- sort(unique(x$Country.Code))
  stopifnot(all(vapply(sets, function(z) setequal(z, codes), logical(1))))
  codes
}
trend_country_count <- function(label, indicator = "U5MR") {
  length(trend_country_codes(trend_country_projection, label, indicator))
}

national_rate_2021 <- function(code, shortind) {
  value <- national_rates_2022$Median[
    national_rates_2022$ISO.Code == code &
      national_rates_2022$Shortind == shortind &
      national_rates_2022$Sex == "Total" &
      national_rates_2022$Year == 2021.5
  ]
  if (length(value) != 1L) {
    stop("Expected one 2021 national estimate for ", code, " / ", shortind)
  }
  value
}
national_decline_2000_2021 <- function(code, shortind) {
  values <- national_rates_2022[
    national_rates_2022$ISO.Code == code &
      national_rates_2022$Shortind == shortind &
      national_rates_2022$Sex == "Total" &
      national_rates_2022$Year %in% c(2000.5, 2021.5),
  ]
  start <- values$Median[values$Year == 2000.5]
  end <- values$Median[values$Year == 2021.5]
  100 * (start - end) / start
}
subnational_rate_range_2021 <- function(code, shortind, admin_level) {
  values <- subnational_estimates_2022$Median[
    subnational_estimates_2022$Country.Code == code &
      subnational_estimates_2022$Shortind == shortind &
      subnational_estimates_2022$Admin.Level == admin_level &
      subnational_estimates_2022$Year == 2021.5
  ]
  c(min = min(values, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(values, na.rm = TRUE))
}
subnational_decline_range_2000_2021 <- function(
  code, shortind, admin_level
) {
  values <- subnational_estimates_2022[
    subnational_estimates_2022$Country.Code == code &
      subnational_estimates_2022$Shortind == shortind &
      subnational_estimates_2022$Admin.Level == admin_level &
      subnational_estimates_2022$Year %in% c(2000.5, 2021.5),
    c("ISO.Internal", "Year", "Median")
  ]
  start <- values[
    values$Year == 2000.5,
    c("ISO.Internal", "Median")
  ]
  end <- values[
    values$Year == 2021.5,
    c("ISO.Internal", "Median")
  ]
  names(start)[2] <- "start"
  names(end)[2] <- "end"
  paired <- merge(start, end, by = "ISO.Internal")
  declines <- 100 * (paired$start - paired$end) / paired$start
  c(min = min(declines), max = max(declines))
}

page64_selected_rows <- function(supplement_names, eurostat_names) {
  supplement_rows <- subnational_supplement[
    subnational_supplement$Country %in% supplement_names,
    c("Country", "Region", "Year", "U5MR")
  ]
  supplement_rows$ISO3Code <- unname(
    supplement_iso[supplement_rows$Country]
  )

  eurostat_rows <- eurostat_nuts1[
    eurostat_nuts1$Country %in% eurostat_countries &
      eurostat_nuts1$Country %in% eurostat_names,
    c("Country", "region.code", "TIME_PERIOD", "U5MR", "ISO3Code")
  ]
  names(eurostat_rows)[
    names(eurostat_rows) == "region.code"
  ] <- "Region"
  names(eurostat_rows)[
    names(eurostat_rows) == "TIME_PERIOD"
  ] <- "Year"

  rbind(supplement_rows, eurostat_rows)
}

page64_region_summary <- function(data) {
  countries <- sort(unique(data$Country))
  data.frame(
    Country = countries,
    regions = vapply(
      countries,
      function(country) {
        length(unique(data$Region[data$Country == country]))
      },
      integer(1)
    ),
    above_target = vapply(
      countries,
      function(country) {
        rows <- data[data$Country == country, ]
        rows <- rows[!duplicated(rows$Region), ]
        sum(rows$U5MR > page64_target, na.rm = TRUE)
      },
      integer(1)
    ),
    ratio = vapply(
      countries,
      function(country) {
        values <- data$U5MR[data$Country == country]
        # Missing rates prevent a complete-country ranking; a zero minimum
        # makes the ratio undefined. Retain regions for availability counts.
        if (any(!is.finite(values)) || min(values) <= 0) return(NA_real_)
        max(values) / min(values)
      },
      numeric(1)
    ),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

page64_country_value <- function(summary, country, column) {
  value <- summary[
    summary$Country == country,
    column,
    drop = TRUE
  ]
  if (length(value) != 1L || is.na(value)) {
    stop("Expected one page-64 value for ", country, " / ", column)
  }
  value
}

aggregate_groups <- function(equity, indicator, groups, type = NULL) {
  x <- aggregate[
    aggregate$equity == equity &
      aggregate$Indicator == indicator &
      aggregate$Year == 2024.5 &
      aggregate$Group %in% groups,
  ]
  if (!is.null(type)) {
    x <- x[x$type == type, ]
  }
  x <- x[match(groups, x$Group), ]
  if (nrow(x) != length(groups) || any(is.na(x$Group))) {
    stop(
      "Missing aggregate group for ",
      paste(equity, indicator, paste(groups, collapse = ", "), sep = " / ")
    )
  }
  x
}

rounded_rates <- function(equity, indicator, groups, type = NULL) {
  round(aggregate_groups(equity, indicator, groups, type)$wgt.rate)
}

group_share <- function(
  equity,
  indicator,
  group,
  measure = c("wgt.birth", "wgt.death"),
  type = NULL
) {
  measure <- match.arg(measure)
  x <- aggregate[
    aggregate$equity == equity &
      aggregate$Indicator == indicator &
      aggregate$Year == 2024.5 &
      aggregate$Group != "total",
  ]
  if (!is.null(type)) {
    x <- x[x$type == type, ]
  }
  100 * x[[measure]][x$Group == group] / sum(x[[measure]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

positive_ratios <- function(label, indicator, numerator, denominator) {
  x <- country_ratios(
    country_selected,
    label,
    indicator,
    numerator,
    denominator
  )
  x[x$ratio > 0 & is.finite(x$ratio), ]
}

ratio_range <- function(x, digits = 1, include_median = TRUE) {
  answer <- paste0(
    format_num(min(x$ratio), digits),
    "-",
    format_num(max(x$ratio), digits)
  )
  if (include_median) {
    answer <- paste0(
      answer,
      "; median ",
      format_num(median(x$ratio), digits)
    )
  }
  answer
}

aggregate_rate_ratio <- function(
  equity, indicator, numerator, denominator, type = NULL
) {
  weighted_rate(equity, indicator, numerator, type) /
    weighted_rate(equity, indicator, denominator, type)
}

aggregate_rate_difference <- function(
  equity, indicator, numerator, denominator, type = NULL
) {
  weighted_rate(equity, indicator, numerator, type) -
    weighted_rate(equity, indicator, denominator, type)
}

combined_group_share <- function(
  equity, indicator, groups, measure, type = NULL
) {
  x <- aggregate[
    aggregate$equity == equity &
      aggregate$Indicator == indicator &
      aggregate$Year == 2024.5 &
      aggregate$Group != "total",
  ]
  if (!is.null(type)) x <- x[x$type == type, ]
  100 * sum(x[[measure]][x$Group %in% groups], na.rm = TRUE) /
    sum(x[[measure]], na.rm = TRUE)
}

country_ratio_wording_numerator <- function(condition) {
  floor(country_ratio_wording_scale * mean(condition, na.rm = TRUE))
}

trend_factor <- function(label, group, indicator) {
  x <- trend[
    trend$label == label &
      trend$Group == group &
      trend$Indicator == indicator,
  ]
  if (nrow(x) != 1L) stop("Expected one trend row.")
  x$`2024-2030` / x$`2000-2024`
}

trend_ratio <- function(label, numerator, denominator, indicator, year) {
  x <- trend[trend$label == label & trend$Indicator == indicator, ]
  x[[as.character(year)]][x$Group == numerator] /
    x[[as.character(year)]][x$Group == denominator]
}

calc_html_escape <- function(value) {
  value <- as.character(value)
  unicode_fallbacks <- c(
    "2013" = "-",
    "2014" = "-",
    "2019" = "'",
    "201C" = '"',
    "201D" = '"',
    "2192" = "->",
    "2212" = "-",
    "2265" = ">="
  )
  for (code in names(unicode_fallbacks)) {
    value <- gsub(
      intToUtf8(strtoi(code, base = 16L)),
      unicode_fallbacks[[code]],
      value,
      fixed = TRUE
    )
    value <- gsub(
      paste0("<U+", code, ">"),
      unicode_fallbacks[[code]],
      value,
      fixed = TRUE
    )
  }
  value <- gsub("&", "&amp;", value, fixed = TRUE)
  value <- gsub("<", "&lt;", value, fixed = TRUE)
  value <- gsub(">", "&gt;", value, fixed = TRUE)
  value <- gsub('"', "&quot;", value, fixed = TRUE)
  value
}

calc_value <- function(
  value,
  status,
  digits = NULL,
  prefix = "",
  suffix = "",
  evidence = ""
) {
  if (length(value) != 1L || is.na(value)) {
    stop("Each inline claim must evaluate to one non-missing value.")
  }
  if (is.numeric(value)) {
    if (is.null(digits)) {
      digits <- if (abs(value - round(value)) < 1e-9) 0L else 1L
    }
    display <- formatC(
      value,
      format = "f",
      digits = digits,
      big.mark = ","
    )
  } else {
    display <- as.character(value)
  }
  css_class <- unname(c(
    match = "value-match",
    mismatch = "value-mismatch",
    unavailable = "value-unavailable"
  )[[status]])
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf(
    '<span class="%s" title="%s">%s%s%s</span>',
    css_class,
    calc_html_escape(evidence),
    calc_html_escape(prefix),
    calc_html_escape(display),
    calc_html_escape(suffix)
  ))
}

calc_black <- function(value, ...) calc_value(value, "match", ...)
calc_red <- function(value, ...) calc_value(value, "mismatch", ...)
calc_blue <- function(value, ...) calc_value(value, "unavailable", ...)

mark_xlsx_numbers <- function(value) {
  escaped <- calc_html_escape(ifelse(is.na(value), "", value))
  gsub(
    "([+-]?[0-9]+(?:[.,][0-9]+)*(?:[/-][0-9]+)?)",
    '<span class="value-match" title="An Uneven Chance of Survival - Tables 1-5.xlsx">\\1</span>',
    escaped,
    perl = TRUE
  )
}

render_source_table <- function(sheet_name) {
  x <- readxl::read_excel(
    sources$annex_tables,
    sheet = sheet_name,
    col_names = FALSE,
    .name_repair = "minimal"
  )
  x[] <- lapply(x, mark_xlsx_numbers)
  knitr::kable(
    x,
    format = "html",
    escape = FALSE,
    row.names = FALSE,
    col.names = rep("", ncol(x)),
    table.attr = 'class="table table-striped table-hover source-xlsx-table"'
  )
}

#| label: code-number-formatting

# Frozen printed displays from the existing LAY-C-dtp-11-C_YL extraction:
# tmp/final-alignment/pdf-pages.json, physical pages 26 and 69.
# These are comparison baselines, not calculation inputs.
education_report_displays <- c(
  "code-number-0137" = "62",
  "code-number-0139" = "1.7",
  "code-number-0424" = "2.9"
)

# Re-evaluate the affected comparison colours on every fresh render.
code_number_display <- function(marked_html, occurrence_id) {
  display <- as.character(marked_html)
  if (occurrence_id %in% names(education_report_displays)) {
    reported <- unname(education_report_displays[[occurrence_id]])
    computed <- gsub("<[^>]*>", "", display)
    if (!grepl("value-unavailable", display, fixed = TRUE)) {
      status_class <- if (identical(computed, reported)) "value-match" else "value-mismatch"
      display <- gsub("value-(match|mismatch)", status_class, display)
    }
    display <- sub('<span ', paste0('<span data-reported-display="', reported, '" '), display, fixed = TRUE)
  }
  display <- sub('class="', 'class="code-produced-number ', display, fixed = TRUE)
  display <- sub('<span ', paste0('<span data-code-occurrence="', occurrence_id, '" '), display, fixed = TRUE)
  knitr::asis_output(display)
}

# A workbook lookup is not a calculation. Keep imported numbers, including
# publication and survey years, explicitly regular weight in every source table.
# Reuse the original formatter and change only its HTML presentation attributes.
mark_xlsx_numbers <- local({
  original_number_markup <- mark_xlsx_numbers
  function(value) {
    gsub(
      '<span class="value-match"',
      '<span class="source-imported-number value-match" data-number-origin="source-workbook" style="font-weight: 400 !important"',
      original_number_markup(value), fixed = TRUE
    )
  }
})

# The birth-size MR1t59 chain in 02_produce-aggregate.R restricts NMR to
# U5MR contributors. Verify both rates exist for both size categories.
birth_size_note_sets <- function(contributors) {
  groups <- c("small.vsmall", "av.large")
  rows <- contributors[
    contributors$label == "bsize" & contributors$Group %in% groups &
      contributors$Indicator %in% c("U5MR", "NMR") &
      is.finite(contributors$wgt.rate) & is.finite(contributors$wgt.death) &
      is.finite(contributors$wgt.birth),
  ]
  sets <- setNames(lapply(c("U5MR", "NMR"), function(indicator) {
    x <- rows[rows$Indicator == indicator, ]
    group_sets <- lapply(groups, function(group) unique(x$Country.Code[x$Group == group]))
    if (!setequal(group_sets[[1]], group_sets[[2]])) {
      stop("Birth-size groups have different contributors for ", indicator)
    }
    group_sets[[1]]
  }), c("U5MR", "NMR"))
  sets$MR1t59 <- intersect(sets$U5MR, sets$NMR)
  if (!setequal(sets$MR1t59, sets$U5MR)) {
    stop("Birth-size MR1t59 requires matching NMR data for every U5MR contributor.")
  }
  sets
}

# Printed values are comparison baselines only; computed values come from above.
note_number_registry <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
note_number <- function(value, reported, occurrence_id, evidence, digits = 0L) {
  stopifnot(length(value) == 1L, !is.na(value), nzchar(evidence))
  displayed <- if (is.numeric(value)) {
    formatC(value, format = "f", digits = digits, big.mark = ",")
  } else as.character(value)
  status <- if (identical(displayed, reported)) "match" else "mismatch"
  note_number_registry[[occurrence_id]] <- data.frame(
    occurrence_id = occurrence_id, reported_display = reported,
    computed_value = as.character(value), computed_display = displayed,
    status = status, source = evidence, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  marked <- calc_value(value, status, digits = digits, evidence = evidence)
  marked <- sub('<span ', paste0('<span data-reported-display="',
    calc_html_escape(reported), '" '), marked, fixed = TRUE)
  code_number_display(marked, occurrence_id)
}

**Final comparison with the designed PDF:** *An Uneven Chance of Survival 12072026 LAY-C-dtp-11-C_YL.pdf*.

**Number-marking key:** Bold is reserved for data-backed results returned by inline R. Black indicates agreement with the printed PDF; red indicates a remaining difference. Typed numbers, fixed constants, page/figure identifiers and values copied from the existing table workbook are regular weight. Blue, if present, means unresolved and is never bold. Values read from a structured source are distinguished from independently recomputed results in their source tooltips and the bold-number register. Text and figure/page references have been aligned for comparison. The PDF's annotations are distinguished from its printed numbers.

This version was refreshed after the education source-estimate update. Calculations use the current pipeline outputs; obsolete education-value assertions have been replaced by source-integrity and narrative-consistency checks. The three newly changed displayed results are compared dynamically with the frozen printed values: page 26, education gap reduction and the 2024 disparity ratio; page 69, Nepal's neonatal education disparity ratio. Other pre-existing comparison markings are retained. Tables 1–5 are still imported from the original source XLSX; Table 5 remains in full under page 78. Chart and map artwork remains omitted; the regenerated Figure 8 is available in the project's figures and design folders.

**Scope of this refresh:** all 456 existing inline calculations were rerun against both the previous and updated inputs. This is a data-change review, not a new certification of every printed number, imported table cell or chart/map label. The existing extracted PDF text supplies the comparison baseline; the original designed PDF was not available for a fresh page-by-page review. The separate inequality-index input used for the heatmaps was not regenerated by scripts 01–06.

Page 36 retains the original **<span class="number-literal">2022</span>** ethnicity calculations, so its differences from the PDF's **<span class="number-literal">2024</span>** coverage remain red. No calculation was changed to make a number agree with the PDF.

## Will I survive to age <span class="number-literal">5</span>?

A child born today faces remarkably better chances of survival than one born at the beginning of this century. According to the latest estimates on child mortality, the global under-five mortality rate declined by more than half between 2000 and 2024.<sup>1</sup> The risk of dying during the critical first 28 days of life decreased by `r code_number_display(calc_black(world_nmr_decline, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Region_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0001")` per cent, while older children under age 5 – those aged 1–59 months – are `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(mr_decline), digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Region_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0002")` per cent less likely to die before reaching age 5 than they were in 2000.

Yet progress has not reached every child. In 2024, `r code_number_display(calc_black(world_u5_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Region_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0003")` million children died before reaching their fifth birthday, including `r code_number_display(calc_black(world_nmr_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Region_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0004")` million newborns. These tragedies are increasingly concentrated among the world’s most vulnerable children. Children in the poorest and least developed countries, as well as those living in fragile- and conflict-affected settings, shoulder a disproportionate share of this burden. Unequal chances of survival not only persist across countries, but are also evident within countries themselves.<sup>2</sup>

Due primarily to causes including premature birth, complications around the time of birth and common childhood illnesses (e.g., pneumonia, diarrhoea, malaria), many newborn and under-five deaths are preventable. But further reducing mortality rates – particularly in high-burden settings – requires looking beyond cause of death alone. Policies and programmes must also

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">5</span> {#pdf-page-5 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

address the underlying conditions that shape a child’s chance of survival and reach the most vulnerable children.

Child mortality is deeply influenced by broader social and economic conditions – often through intermediary factors such as maternal health<sup>3 </sup>– and by inequalities in access to services, such as health care and education.<sup>4</sup> With this in mind, pinpointing some of the background factors that determine children’s outcomes in the first five years of life is critical in order to identify which children are at greatest risk and to direct resources, investments and interventions where they can have the greatest impact.

This report identifies seven measurable determinants that mediate child mortality rates. They can be grouped into two broad categories: socio-economic factors (household wealth, maternal education and urban/rural residence) and maternal fertility-related conditions (maternal age, birth interval, birth order and birth size), which are closely interlinked.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">6</span> {#pdf-page-6 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

## What are my chances of making it to my <span class="number-literal">5th</span> birthday if…

- ... I live in one of the world’s poorest households?
- ... My mother never went to school or only attended primary school?
- ... I live in a rural area?
- ... My mother is an adolescent or older than 40?
- ... I’m born within two years of a sibling?
- ... I’m the fourth-born or later child in my family?
- ... I’m a small newborn?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">7</span> {#pdf-page-7 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

Primarily based on household survey data<sup>5</sup> produced by low- and middle-income countries – settings that accounted for over 9 in 10 (`r code_number_display(calc_black(round(coverage_lmic$u5_percent), digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv; LMIC country set"), "code-number-0005")` per cent) under-five deaths in 2024 – this analysis shows that these factors and conditions can increase a child’s risk of dying before age 5 by many degrees. Findings for certain determinants for a select group of high-income countries further demonstrate that children face unjust outcomes across economic settings. Focus boxes on ethnicity, stillbirth and subnational trends highlight the significance of these topics when it comes to understanding equity and under-five mortality rates.

Though the risk factors in this analysis have different levels of data availability (see ‘Annex: Data availability’, `r calc_black(report_pages$data_availability, digits = 0, prefix = "p. ", evidence = "calculated report structure")`),<sup>6</sup> when viewed together, they create a more nuanced understanding of the circumstances that are likely to shape survival to age 5. By zooming out beyond country level and looking at aggregates, the identified disparities in under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality provide

policy- and decision makers with critical guidance on identifying which children are being left behind and some of the reasons why. This report’s findings underscore the need to analyse child health and survival through an equity lens, yielding evidence which can then be used to inform the design, implementation and financing of policies and programmes that ensure the most marginalized and vulnerable children in society are reached.

### Child mortality targets, equity and data disaggregation

The SDGs aim to end preventable deaths of newborns and children younger than age 5 by 2030. All countries should aim to reduce neonatal mortality to at least as low as `r calc_black(sdg_targets$nmr, digits = 0, evidence = "SDG target definition")` deaths per 1,000 live births and under-five mortality to at least as low as `r calc_black(sdg_targets$u5mr, digits = 0, evidence = "SDG target definition")` deaths per 1,000 live births (SDG 3.2). To address inequity and ensure no child is left behind, the SDGs call for data to be disaggregated by many of the risk factors identified in this report.<sup>7</sup>

The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) emphasize the need to address disparities within countries, regardless of a country’s wealth. An approach centred on equity is vital to reaching the SDG targets for neonatal and under-five mortality and achieving an end to preventable child deaths. In order to realize the important vision of the 2030 Agenda and ensure every child’s right to survive to age 5 is upheld, inequities between different groups of children must be recognized, prioritized and rectified for every child in every community.

### A fair chance in life: Equity vs. equality

Equity is achieved when every child has a fair chance in life and can reach their full potential for well-being. It accounts for the fact that different children have different sets of needs based on their backgrounds, individual circumstances and a range of socio-economic factors. Equity is a pillar of sustainable development. Equality refers to circumstances where every child is treated in the same way and supported by the same resources and opportunities.

## Findings and analysis: Why do some children face a higher risk of dying before age <span class="number-literal">5</span>?

## Socio-economic factors

This section examines three socio-economic factors – household wealth, mother’s education level and place of residence (rural versus urban environments) – and their association with survival to age 5. While numerous factors contribute to child mortality outcomes, these dimensions are readily available in household survey data and significantly shape under-five mortality rates.

The findings in this section provide critical evidence to help guide, design and implement solutions that can reduce systemic inequalities within countries and help ensure equal chances for every child during the first five years of life.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">15</span> {#pdf-page-15 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

## Wealth: What if I live in a poor household?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">16</span> {#pdf-page-16 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

Wealth can shape many aspects critical to child survival, such as parents’ ability to afford health care, nutritious food and safer environments for children.

The impact of wealth-related deprivations becomes more visible as children age, with higher mortality rates among the poorest older cohort of children (1–59 months) than among the poorest newborns.

This analysis considers wealth as a measure of household wealth (as opposed to measures of absolute poverty). Populations of children are grouped into five quintiles – poorest to richest – defined by country-specific ranges. The latest United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME) numbers are used to project under-five mortality rates by wealth quintile to 2030.

The availability of trend estimates by wealth quintile also allowed for a deeper analysis of the relationship between household wealth and under-five mortality rates – reaffirming the need for better data across the dimensions highlighted in this report to inform proactive equitable and effective action for children.

Almost `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("children_multidimensional_poverty_millions"), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0037")` million children in developing countries live in multidimensional poverty, without even a minimum level of access to education, health services, housing, nutrition, sanitation or safe drinking water.<sup>8</sup>

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">17</span> {#pdf-page-17 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### Children from the poorest households are, on average, nearly <span class="number-literal">twice</span> as likely to die before reaching age <span class="number-literal">5</span> than those from the wealthiest households

### Figure <span class="number-literal">1</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by household wealth (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: Under-five mortality rates are not strictly comparable with the neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates in this analysis since different methods were applied to calculate them. The under-five mortality rate by wealth quintile was modelled by UN IGME for `r note_number(length(note_country_sets$wealth$U5MR), "106", "note-fig01-u5-countries", "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv; distinct ISO3Code", digits = 0)` low- and middle-income countries using survey data as input, while neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates are based on analysis of DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources for `r note_number(length(note_country_sets$wealth$NMR), "68", "note-fig01-nmr-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` low- and middle-income countries.

The risk of dying before age 5 for children growing up in the poorest households is on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Wealth quintile', 'U5MR', '1.quintile', '5.quintile'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0038")` times that of children from the richest households. In 2024, the average estimated under-five mortality rate was `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Wealth quintile', 'U5MR', '1.quintile'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0039")` deaths per 1,000 live births in the poorest quintile, compared to `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Wealth quintile', 'U5MR', '5.quintile'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0040")` deaths per 1,000 live births in the wealthiest quintile, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Wealth quintile', 'U5MR', '1.quintile', '5.quintile'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0041")` deaths per 1,000 live births (see Figure 1).

The neonatal mortality rate in the poorest households was only slightly higher than in the wealthiest households, with an average ratio of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Wealth quintile', 'NMR', '1.quintile', '5.quintile'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0042")` and an absolute difference of only `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Wealth quintile', 'NMR', '1.quintile', '5.quintile'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0043")` deaths per 1,000 live births. Among the older under-five age group, differences by wealth quintile become more pronounced: the 1–59-months mortality rate for children in the poorest households was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Wealth quintile', 'MR1t59', '1.quintile', '5.quintile'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0044")` times that of children living in the wealthiest households, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Wealth quintile', 'MR1t59', '1.quintile', '5.quintile'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0045")` deaths per 1,000 children aged 28 days.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">18</span> {#pdf-page-18 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### The poorest children in low- and middle-income countries bear a disproportionate burden of under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths

### Figure <span class="number-literal">2</span>. Percentage of live births and under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths, by household wealth (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Children in the poorest wealth quintile account for a larger proportion of under-five deaths compared to their share of live births. Although births are equally distributed by quintile in our analysis (see Figure 2), deaths are not: Nearly half of all under-five deaths (`r code_number_display(calc_black(combined_group_share('Wealth quintile', 'U5MR', c('1.quintile', '2.quintile'), 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0046")` per cent) occurred among children born into the two poorest groups, compared to `r code_number_display(calc_black(combined_group_share('Wealth quintile', 'U5MR', c('4.quintile', '5.quintile'), 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0047")` per cent in the two wealthiest groups.

## Disparity ratios and wealth: How pronounced are inequities between different groups of children within countries?

### Figure <span class="number-literal">3</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rates, neonatal mortality rates and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rates in the poorest and wealthiest households in selected countries

While the comparative risk of dying before age 5 in the poorest and wealthiest households varies by country, under-five mortality is consistently associated with household wealth in all countries analysed (see &lt;childmortality.org&gt; for country charts and data). In every country, child mortality was highest among the poorest quintile and lowest among the wealthiest quintile.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">19</span> {#pdf-page-19 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

In 2024, the under-five mortality rate disparity ratio between children in the poorest households and children in the wealthiest households across countries ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(wealth_u5$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0048")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(wealth_u5$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0049")`, with a median ratio of `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(wealth_u5$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0050")` across countries.

In three quarters of countries (`r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_u5_at_or_below_upper_band_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0051")`), children born in the poorest households were `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(wealth_u5$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0052")` to `r calc_black(wealth_ratio_upper_band, digits = 1, evidence = "analysis band")` times more likely to die before age 5 than children born in the wealthiest ones (see Figure 3). In one quarter of countries (`r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_u5_above_upper_band_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0054")`), the ratio was higher than 2. In absolute terms, the difference between the poorest and richest households was more than `r calc_black(wealth_difference_cutoff, digits = 0, evidence = "analysis cutoff")` deaths per 1,000 live births in `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_u5_difference_above_cutoff_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0056")` per cent of the countries (`r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_u5_difference_above_cutoff_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0057")`), ranging overall from the smallest difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(wealth_u5_difference), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0058")` deaths per 1,000 live births to the largest difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(wealth_u5_difference), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0059")` deaths per 1,000 live births.

For the neonatal mortality rate, half of the countries (`r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_nmr_below_median_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0060")`) had a disparity ratio of less than `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(wealth_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0061")` between babies born to the poorest households and those born to the richest households.

The ratios increased among the older under-five age group, with the 1–59-months mortality rate disparity ratio between the poorest and wealthiest households exceeding `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(wealth_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0062")` in half of the countries (`r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_mr_above_median_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0063")`).

## Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality, wealth and the SDGs

### If the SDG targets were achieved by <span class="number-literal">2030</span> across all wealth quintiles, `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_lives_saved_total / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0073")` <span class="number-literal">million</span> lives could be saved

### Figure <span class="number-literal">5</span>. Estimated and projected under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rates in the poorest and the wealthiest quintiles, by different scenarios (<span class="number-literal">1990</span>–<span class="number-literal">2030</span>)

Note: The ‘achieve SDG target by 2030’ scenarios are applied at the country level. Countries that have already met the SDG target continue their current downward trends, resulting in an aggregate rate below 25 deaths per 1,000 live births.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">21</span> {#pdf-page-21 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

From 1990 to 2024, the gap in mortality rates between the poorest and wealthiest populations saw a notable decline in absolute terms. If this trajectory continues, the difference is expected to further reduce to `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_2030_current_q1 - wealth_2030_current_q5, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0074")` deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030, with an under-five mortality rate of `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_2030_current_q1, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0075")` deaths per 1,000 live births in the poorest households and `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_2030_current_q5, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0076")` deaths per 1,000 live births in the richest households (see Figure 5). While absolute differences are expected to decline, relative differences are projected to remain: By 2030, children born into the poorest quintile will continue to face a risk of dying before age 5 `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_2030_current_ratio_word, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0077")` that of children in the wealthiest quintile.

Achieving the SDG under-five mortality target on time across wealth quintile groups in the `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_country_count, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0078")` countries analysed would save the lives of `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_lives_saved_total / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0079")` million children from now until 2030; almost `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_lives_saved_q1_q2_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0080")` per cent of these children would come from the two poorest quintiles, with a third (`r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_lives_saved_q1 / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0081")` million) in the poorest quintile alone. By 2024, `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(100 * wealth_met_2024[[1]] / wealth_country_count), digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0082")` per cent (`r note_number(wealth_met_2024[[1]], "36", "country-p21-poorest-target", "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv")`) of the poorest quintiles in the countries analysed had already met the SDG target, compared to `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(100 * wealth_met_2024[[5]] / wealth_country_count), digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0083")` per cent (`r note_number(wealth_met_2024[[5]], "59", "country-p21-richest-target", "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv")`) of the wealthiest quintiles.

Comparing progress in reducing under-five mortality rates at the national level to progress by wealth quintile, `r code_number_display(calc_black(national_off_track_wealth_countries, digits = 0, evidence = "UN IGME 2025 Countries Obs.Req.ARR and Status_long.csv"), "code-number-0084")` countries among the `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_country_count, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0085")` countries are off track at the national level to reach the under-five mortality target, while `r code_number_display(calc_black(off_track_counts[[1]], digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0086")` are off track in the poorest quintile, `r code_number_display(calc_black(off_track_counts[[2]], digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0087")` in the second-poorest quintile, `r code_number_display(calc_black(off_track_counts[[3]], digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0088")` in the middle quintile, `r code_number_display(calc_black(off_track_counts[[4]], digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0089")` in the second-wealthiest quintile and `r code_number_display(calc_black(off_track_counts[[5]], digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0090")` in the wealthiest quintile.

To achieve the SDG target on time, the wealthiest quintile needs to accelerate its current annual rate of reduction by about `r code_number_display(calc_red(wealth_acceleration$Factor[[5]], digits = 1, suffix = " times", evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0091")`, the second-wealthiest quintile by `r code_number_display(calc_red(wealth_acceleration$Factor[[4]], digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0092")` times, the middle quintile by `r code_number_display(calc_red(wealth_acceleration$Factor[[3]], digits = 1, suffix = " times", evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0093")`, the second-poorest quintile by `r code_number_display(calc_red(wealth_acceleration$Factor[[2]], digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0094")` times and the poorest quintile by `r code_number_display(calc_red(wealth_acceleration$Factor[[1]], digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0095")` times. These findings show that current progress in many countries is insufficient even among the wealthiest households, highlighting the need for accelerated progress across all quintiles.

If the SDG target for under-five mortality was achieved for the children born in the poorest and richest quintiles in each country, the gap between their under-five mortality rates at aggregated level would narrow to just `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_acceleration$U5MR_2030_SDG[[1]] - wealth_acceleration$U5MR_2030_SDG[[5]], digits = 1, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_world.csv"), "code-number-0096")` deaths per 1,000 live births by 2030 – a far more equitable outcome for children. This captures the immense value of looking at vulnerable subgroups when examining progress towards SDG targets, whether by socio-economic group, subnational level or otherwise.

For further details, please see the Annex.

## Why is data availability important?

Data and statistical systems play a critical role in identifying the groups of children experiencing the highest rates of mortality. Well-functioning and high-quality data collection mechanisms enable countries and organizations to track and monitor the well-being of children, understand where inequities persist and channel resources to reach those children left behind.

Survey data in low- and middle-income countries provide vital insights into these disparities. These data are often not timely, however, but refer to the 5- or 10-year period before the survey. For under-five mortality estimation by wealth in this report, for instance, the average for most recent data point from surveys was `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_u5_age, digits = 1, evidence = "dataset_formodeling_2026-02-03.csv"), "code-number-0107")` years old (from target year 2024) across the `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_country_count, digits = 0, evidence = "IGME2025_U5MR_wealth_quintile_projection_country.csv"), "code-number-0108")` countries. For neonatal and 1–59-months mortality estimation, the average for most recent data point was `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_nmr_age, digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0109")` years old across the `r code_number_display(calc_black(length(unique(wealth_nmr$Country.Code)), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0110")` countries.

These data gaps must be addressed in order to identify where and which children face unequal chances of survival.

## Education: What if my mother never went to school or only attended primary school?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">24</span> {#pdf-page-24 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

Upholding the right of girls to go to school carries broad ripple effects in society. Research demonstrates that when girls are educated, poverty rates decline, maternal health improves, violence decreases and children’s chances of survival increase. Maternal levels of education have been consistently linked to child mortality rates.<sup>9, 10</sup>

Around the world, `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("girls_out_of_school_millions"), digits = 1, suffix = " million", evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0111")` girls are out of school – `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("girls_primary_out_of_school_millions"), digits = 1, suffix = " million", evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0112")` girls of primary school age and `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("girls_secondary_out_of_school_millions"), digits = 1, suffix = " million", evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0113")` girls of secondary school age. Girls in countries affected by conflict are more than twice as likely to be out of school than those living in non-affected countries.<sup>11</sup>

### The less education a mother has, the more likely she is to endure the loss of a child

### Figure <span class="number-literal">6</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by mother’s education (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: Two standard groupings for mother’s education were used in all countries: `r calc_black(figure6_first_grouping_number, digits = 0, evidence = "Figure 6 grouping definition")`) two categories: no education or primary, and secondary or higher, or `r calc_black(figure6_second_grouping_number, digits = 0, evidence = "Figure 6 grouping definition")`) four categories: no education, primary, secondary, and higher. The dotted line separates the two standard groupings. The under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates by mother’s education for the first grouping (two categories) are derived from UNICEF analysis based on DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources for `r code_number_display(calc_black(nrow(education_u5_detail), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0116")` countries; `r code_number_display(calc_black(education_four_group_country_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0117")` of these also had data for the second grouping (four categories).

Children born to mothers with no education or only primary education are more likely to die before they turn `r calc_black(child_age_limit, digits = 0, evidence = "under-five indicator definition")` years old than those born to a mother with secondary or higher education. These risks become more pronounced as children age: Among mothers with the lowest levels of education, mortality rates are higher among children aged 1–59 months than among newborns. The opposite

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">25</span> {#pdf-page-25 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

is true, however, among children born to mothers with higher levels of education, whose chances of survival improve as they age.

For the `r code_number_display(calc_black(nrow(education_u5_detail), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0119")` countries analysed, the under-five mortality rate was `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'noedu.primary', type = 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0120")` deaths per 1,000 live births for children of mothers with no or primary education, and `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'sec.higher', type = 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0121")` deaths per 1,000 live births for children of mothers with secondary or higher education (see Figure 6). The risk of dying for children born to mothers in the combined two lowest education levels was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'noedu.primary', 'sec.higher', 'combined all countries'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0122")` times that of those born to mothers in the two combined highest education levels, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'noedu.primary', 'sec.higher', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0123")` deaths per 1,000 live births.

The neonatal mortality rate for children whose mothers had no or only primary education was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio("Mother's education", 'NMR', 'noedu.primary', 'sec.higher', 'combined all countries'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0124")` times that of those with mothers who attended secondary or higher education, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference("Mother's education", 'NMR', 'noedu.primary', 'sec.higher', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0125")` deaths per 1,000 live births. Older children face even higher risks: The 1–59-months mortality rate for children of mothers with no or primary education was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio("Mother's education", 'MR1t59', 'noedu.primary', 'sec.higher', 'combined all countries'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0126")` times that of children born to mothers with secondary or higher education, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference("Mother's education", 'MR1t59', 'noedu.primary', 'sec.higher', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0127")` deaths per 1,000 children aged 28 days.

More detailed information from a subset of countries shows that mortality rates gradually decline as levels of maternal education increase. In this subset of data, under-five mortality rates in 2024 were `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'noeducation', type = '4 groups'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0128")` deaths per 1,000 live births for the group with no maternal education, and `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(education_primary_u5), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0129")`, `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'secondary', type = '4 groups'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0130")` and `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'higher', type = '4 groups'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0131")` deaths per 1,000 live births for children of mothers with primary, secondary and higher education, respectively.

### The burden of under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths is unequally carried by mothers with little to no education

### Figure <span class="number-literal">7</span>. Percentage of live births, under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths, neonatal deaths and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months deaths, by mother’s education (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Mothers with the least education shoulder a disproportionate share of under-five deaths, with lower levels of maternal education (no education/primary) associated with a higher percentage of under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months deaths compared to the share of live births. Although `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'noedu.primary', 'wgt.birth', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0132")` per cent of live births occur in this group, children born to mothers with the least education

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">26</span> {#pdf-page-26 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

accounted for `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'noedu.primary', 'wgt.death', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0133")` per cent of all under-five deaths in 2024. Children born to mothers with secondary or higher education, however, accounted for `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'sec.higher', 'wgt.birth', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0134")` per cent of live births in 2024, compared to just `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's education", 'U5MR', 'sec.higher', 'wgt.death', 'combined all countries'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0135")` per cent of under-five deaths (see Figure 7).

### Children of mothers with lower education continue to be disadvantaged

Under-five mortality rates declined across all education levels and both age groups (neonates, 1–59-month-olds) in the aggregate for `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_country_count('edu_group_2'), digits = 0, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0136")` countries with trend data since 2000. While the absolute difference in the under-five mortality rate between children of mothers with no or primary education and those with secondary or higher education dropped by `r code_number_display(calc_black(education_gap_decline, digits = 0, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0137")` per cent, the decline in disparity ratio was smaller – from around `r code_number_display(calc_black(education_ratio_2000, digits = 1, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0138")` in 2000 to `r code_number_display(calc_black(education_ratio_2024, digits = 1, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0139")` in 2024.

Reaching the under-five mortality SDG targets for all children regardless of their mother’s level of education will require concentrated efforts among the groups that are off track to meet the target – that is, mothers with no, primary or secondary education. In the two lowest levels of education, the current annual rate of reduction would need to accelerate by a factor of six in under-five mortality and by more than eight times for neonatal mortality to meet the SDG targets by 2030.

## Disparity ratios and mother’s education: How pronounced are inequities between different groups of children within countries?

### Figure <span class="number-literal">8</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rates, neonatal mortality rates and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rates by mother’s education in selected countries

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">27</span> {#pdf-page-27 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

Within countries, the under-five mortality disparity ratio by mother’s level of education increases as children age, with greater disparities observed among older children under age 5 than newborns. Lower maternal educational attainment is generally associated with higher mortality risks, but variation exists across countries (see <https://childmortality.org> for country charts and data).

Among the countries analysed, the under-five mortality disparity ratio in 2024 of children born to mothers with no or primary education compared to those born to mothers with secondary or higher education ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(education_u5_detail$ratio), digits = 2, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0140")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(education_u5_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0141")`. Nearly half of the countries showed a ratio greater than `r calc_black(education_ratio_threshold, digits = 1, evidence = "analysis threshold")`.

The neonatal mortality disparity ratio for children of mothers with no or primary education and those of mothers with secondary or higher education ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(education_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0143")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(education_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0144")`. The ratio was above `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(education_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0145")` for nearly half of countries analysed.

When it comes to older children, the range ticked even higher: The 1–59-months mortality disparity ratio for children born to mothers with no or primary education and those born to mothers with secondary or higher education ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(education_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0146")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(education_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0147")`. The median ratio was `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(education_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0148")`.

### BEHIND THE DATA: MEASURING CHILD MORTALITY AND MOTHER’S EDUCATION

### Map <span class="number-literal">2</span>. Countries with available survey or sample vital registration data for mother’s education level analysis

Note: This map does not reflect a position by UNICEF on the legal status of any country or territory or the delimitation of any frontiers.

The analysis of mortality by mother’s education is based on data from `r note_number(coverage_education$countries, "66", "note-map02-education-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; distinct education U5MR aggregate contributors", digits = 0)` low- and middle-income countries, where `r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$u5_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0149")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$u5_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0150")` million) of the world’s under-five deaths, `r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$nmr_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0151")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$nmr_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0152")` million) of neonatal deaths, `r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$mr1t59_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0153")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$mr1t59_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0154")` million) of deaths among children aged 1–59 months and `r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$birth_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "data_livebirths.csv"), "code-number-0155")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_education$births / 1e6, digits = 0, evidence = "data_livebirths.csv"), "code-number-0156")` million) of live births took place in 2024. The trend analysis was based on data for `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_country_count('edu_group_2'), digits = 0, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0157")` countries with three or more data points. For mother’s education groupings, the highest level of education attended – not necessarily completed – was used. Two standard groupings for mother’s education were used in all countries: 1) one grouping of two categories (no or primary education, and secondary or higher education) for `r code_number_display(calc_black(nrow(education_u5_detail), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0158")` countries; and 2) a second grouping of four categories (no, primary, secondary, or higher education) for a subset of `r code_number_display(calc_black(education_four_group_country_count, digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0159")` countries. If there were insufficient data to calculate mortality rates by mother’s education in the 5-year period before the survey, a 10-year period was used. If the data were still insufficient, they were regrouped into two broader groups: no education or primary, and secondary or higher education. In cases where this reclassification was not feasible, survey data from that country were excluded. Survey data with national education categories were reclassified to match the standard categories, if possible.
