## Residence: What if my home is in a rural area?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">29</span> {#pdf-page-29 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

The world has become increasingly urban; more people live in cities today than in towns or rural areas.<sup>12</sup>

### A child growing up in a rural setting is far less likely to see their <span class="number-literal">fifth</span> birthday than a child in an urban <span class="number-literal">one</span>

### Figure <span class="number-literal">9</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by residence (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: The under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates by residence are derived from UNICEF analysis based on DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources for `r note_number(length(note_country_sets$residence$U5MR), "67", "note-fig09-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` countries.

Children born in rural settings die more often than those born in urban environments: In 2024, the under-five mortality rate in rural areas was `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Residence', 'U5MR', 'rural'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0160")` deaths per 1,000 live births versus `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Residence', 'U5MR', 'urban'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0161")` deaths per 1,000 live births in urban areas (see Figure 9). The likelihood that a child will die before age 5 in a rural area was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Residence', 'U5MR', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0162")` times greater than that of a child growing up in an urban area, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Residence', 'U5MR', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0163")` deaths per 1,000 live births. This gap in survival is wider among children aged 1–59 months than it is during the first 28 days of life.

Newborns living in rural environments faced a risk of dying an average of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Residence', 'NMR', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0164")` times that of those living in urban settings, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Residence', 'NMR', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0165")` deaths per 1,000 live births. Meanwhile, the 1–59-months mortality rate for children in rural areas was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Residence', 'MR1t59', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0166")` times as high as that of children in urban areas, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Residence', 'MR1t59', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0167")` deaths per 1,000 children aged 28 days.

Due to factors like poor access to and coverage of health care, limited basic sanitation and lower education levels, children in rural areas have long faced higher risks of mortality than their urban counterparts. While an increasing number of children are growing up in urban slums, under-five mortality rates remain, on average, higher in rural than in urban areas.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">30</span> {#pdf-page-30 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### Rural settings experience a disproportionate number of under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths

### Figure <span class="number-literal">10</span>. Percentage of live births, under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths, neonatal deaths and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months deaths, by residence (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Children in rural areas account for an unequal share of under-five deaths: While `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Residence', 'U5MR', 'rural', 'wgt.birth'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0168")` per cent of live births in 2024 occurred in rural areas, these regions accounted for `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Residence', 'U5MR', 'rural', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0169")` per cent of under-five deaths (see Figure 10). Meanwhile, `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Residence', 'NMR', 'rural', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0170")` per cent of neonatal deaths were in rural areas and an even higher proportion – `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Residence', 'MR1t59', 'rural', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0171")` per cent – of deaths among 1–59-month-olds took place in these settings.

## Children in rural areas are still being left behind

Since 2000, under-five mortality rates in rural and urban areas have declined by a similar percentage based on `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_country_count('residence'), digits = 0, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0172")` countries with trend data. The absolute difference in under-five mortality rates declined by almost half between children in rural and urban areas, while the relative disadvantage in rural areas remained at similar levels between 2000 and 2024, with children living in rural areas facing a risk of dying in the first five years of life `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Residence', 'U5MR', 'rural', 'urban'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0173")` times that of children living in urban areas.

Achieving the under-five mortality SDG target will require a focus on rural areas: On average, the current annual rate of reduction in rural areas needs to more than quintuple to meet the target by 2030, compared to the `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_factor('residence', 'urban', 'U5MR'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregates_2000_2024_from_extrapolation_benchmarked.xlsx"), "code-number-0174")`-times increase needed in urban areas. Interventions targeting children aged 1–59 months are crucial given the larger rural/urban disparities that exist in this age group.

## Disparity ratios and residence: How pronounced are inequities between different groups of children within countries?

In most countries, children in rural areas are disadvantaged compared to children in urban areas (see Figure 11). The under-five mortality rate disparity ratio of rural to urban areas ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(residence_u5_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0175")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(residence_u5_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0176")`, with a range of `r code_number_display(calc_black(quantile(residence_u5_detail$ratio, 0.25), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0177")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(quantile(residence_u5_detail$ratio, 0.75), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0178")` in half of the countries.

The neonatal mortality rate disparity ratio of rural to urban environments ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(residence_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0179")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(residence_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0180")`. The middle half of countries fell between `r code_number_display(calc_black(quantile(residence_nmr_detail$ratio, 0.25), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0181")` and `r code_number_display(calc_black(quantile(residence_nmr_detail$ratio, 0.75), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0182")`. The 1–59-months mortality rate disparity ratio of rural to urban areas ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(residence_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0183")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(residence_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0184")`, a considerably wider range than that of neonates. The median ratio was also higher in this age group, at `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(residence_mr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0185")` across countries.

set difference from aggregate contributors")` countries – including the two most populous, China and India, along with Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, the Comoros, Kazakhstan, Liberia and Viet Nam – were not included in the aggregates, since the distribution of births by residence was not available from their sample vital registration or survey data. The trend analysis was based on data for `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_country_count('residence'), digits = 0, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0205")` countries with three or more data points. Definitions of ‘rural’ and ‘urban’ are country-specific and reflect those used at the time of the survey. Significant differences exist as to the size of an area defined as ‘urban’, ranging from a population threshold of 200 (in Denmark and Sweden) to `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("urban_threshold_mali"), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0206")` (Mali) or `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("urban_threshold_japan"), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0207")` (Japan). Most countries used a threshold of between 2,000 and `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("urban_threshold_common_upper"), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0208")`.<sup>13</sup>

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">32</span> {#pdf-page-32 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

## As cities grow, what are the implications for under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality among the urban poor?

Based on current trends, by 2050, approximately `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("urban_share_2050_percent"), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0209")` per cent of the global population, or `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("urban_population_2050_billions"), digits = 1, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0210")` billion people, will live in cities.<sup>14</sup> Though data regularly show that urban children have access to better essential services – e.g., health care, education, and water and sanitation – than their rural peers, this advantage often disappears for the poorest urban children. Using a household wealth lens to examine under-five mortality rates among urban children, a study shows that in some countries, the most disadvantaged urban children are more likely to die before turning 5 than those in rural areas.<sup>15</sup>

Data and evidence from sub-Saharan Africa, where rapid urbanization is taking place, provide important insights as to how urbanization, household wealth and access to health care might converge to shape the chances of survival to age 5. As sub-Saharan Africa’s capital cities expand, health care coverage – particularly in slums – has not kept pace, and is in some cases progressing more slowly than in rural areas.<sup>16</sup> This has led to concerning outcomes in child mortality in some countries, where children in the poorest urban quintile are at least twice as likely to die before their fifth birthday as their richest urban peers.<sup>17</sup>

These trends illustrate the importance of examining what happens when particular factors that shape under-five mortality intersect – in this case, examining household wealth in tandem with residence in order to determine which children face the greatest risks of death before age 5.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">33</span> {#pdf-page-33 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

**CRITICAL FOCUS**

## Ethnicity and under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality

Though the SDGs call for disaggregation of social indicators by ethnic group, the evidence base currently lacks robust, systematic, multi-country analyses of ethnic inequalities in child health and survival. But to realize the vision of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and end preventable child deaths, it is vital that these analyses are regularly conducted and that action is taken accordingly.<sup>18 </sup>

Around the world and across economic settings, ethnicity is influencing whether or not a child survives to age 5.<sup>19</sup> Ethnicity has been tied to lower rates of immunization among different groups of children, disproportionate rates of preventable childhood diseases and unequal access to essential services like health care, education, and water, sanitation and hygiene – all of which can affect survival to age 5.<sup>20 </sup>

In some countries, members of particular ethnic minority groups are disadvantaged;<sup>21, 22, 23</sup> in others, children from the ethnic majority experience an imbalance in child mortality outcomes.<sup>24, 25</sup> Ethnicity can also mediate under-five mortality rates in wealthier countries. Due to large uncertainty in the data driven by small case numbers, however, these differences are often not statistically significant.

This box examines under-five mortality rates by ethnic group in `r note_number(length(note_ethnicity_example_codes), "3", "country-p33-survey-examples", "ethnicity dataset_0522.csv; available selected ETH/NPL/MRT examples")` low- and lower-middle-income countries (Ethiopia, Nepal and Mauritania) and `r note_number(length(note_ethnicity_hic_example_countries), "2", "country-p33-hic-examples", "ethnicity_hic; Sheet2; distinct Country")` upper-middle- and high-income countries (Australia and Brazil). The findings illustrate the need for country-specific analyses of ethnicity across country income groups in order to ensure equal chances of survival for every child.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">34</span> {#pdf-page-34 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

The black line represents the standard error.

Under-five mortality rates by ethnic group were analysed for `r note_number(ethnicity_coverage$countries, "42", "note-p36-ethnicity-countries", "ethnicity dataset_0522.csv; distinct ISO3Code", digits = 0)` low- and middle-income countries, building on previous UNICEF analysis.<sup>26 </sup>Approximately `r code_number_display(calc_black(ethnicity_coverage$u5_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0221")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(ethnicity_coverage$u5_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0222")` million) of global under-five deaths and `r code_number_display(calc_black(ethnicity_coverage$birth_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "data_livebirths.csv"), "code-number-0223")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(ethnicity_coverage$births / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "data_livebirths.csv"), "code-number-0224")` million) of live births in <span class="number-literal">2024</span> occurred in these countries. Ethnic diversity varied from `r note_number(ethnicity_min_groups, "3", "p36-min-ethnic-groups", "ethnicity dataset_0522.csv; minimum distinct ethnic-group count by ISO3Code")` groups (`r note_number(ethnicity_extreme_country_names(ethnicity_min_groups), "Guatemala", "p36-min-ethnic-group-countries", "ethnicity dataset_0522.csv; all countries tied for minimum distinct ethnic-group count")`) to `r note_number(ethnicity_max_groups, "43", "p36-max-ethnic-groups", "ethnicity dataset_0522.csv; maximum distinct ethnic-group count by ISO3Code")` groups (`r note_number(ethnicity_extreme_country_names(ethnicity_max_groups), "Cameroon", "p36-max-ethnic-group-countries", "ethnicity dataset_0522.csv; all countries tied for maximum distinct ethnic-group count")`) in the dataset. The definition of ‘ethnicity’ in this analysis was broad. It included self-reported ethnic affiliation, language, skin colour (South Africa), and caste or tribal group (India). All mortality rates refer to the 10-year period leading up to the year the survey was taken; ethnic groups with less than `r calc_black(ethnicity_case_threshold, digits = 0, evidence = "analysis inclusion rule")` weighted cases in the survey were excluded. Mortality estimates from survey data by ethnic group are in many cases less precise, with a coefficient of variation above `r calc_black(ethnicity_cv_threshold, digits = 0, evidence = "analysis precision rule")` per cent, rendering comparison between ethnic groups less accurate.

## Maternal fertility-related conditions

This section examines four maternal fertility-related conditions – mother’s age, birth interval, birth order and birth size – that are tied to higher risks of under-five mortality. While these factors are discussed individually, it is important to note that three of them – mother’s age, birth interval and birth order – are often interrelated.<sup>27</sup> For further discussion of these links, see p. 53.

The patterns described in this section reiterate the need for every mother-to-be to know the risks and benefits associated with pregnancy during different times in her life and receive the care she needs accordingly.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">38</span> {#pdf-page-38 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

## Mother’s age: What if my mother is an adolescent or older than <span class="number-literal">40</span>?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">39</span> {#pdf-page-39 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

The age at which pregnancy occurs carries critical implications for under-five mortality, with children born to the youngest and oldest mothers facing a higher likelihood of death before age 5.<sup>28, 29, 30, 31</sup> Among adolescent mothers, these risks can be seen from the neonatal period until age 5, and also manifest in the incidence of stillbirths (see p. 55).

The effect of maternal age on child survival highlights important issues regarding health-seeking behaviour – particularly among adolescents – and the need to provide access to sexual and reproductive health education. It also reiterates the need to ensure that girls go to school and are protected from child marriage, both of which can be tied to pregnancy during adolescence.

Approximately `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(external_value("adolescent_births_2024_millions")), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0227")` million babies were born to mothers between the ages of 15 and 19 in 2024,<sup>32</sup> about half of them in sub-Saharan Africa. While the global adolescent birth rate has dropped by nearly half since 1994 – declining from 73 to `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("adolescent_birth_rate_2024"), digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0228")` births per 1,000 girls and young women aged 15–19 years – in sub-Saharan Africa, it remains above `r code_number_display(calc_black(floor(external_value("adolescent_birth_rate_ssa_2024") / 10) * 10, digits = 0, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0229")` births per 1,000 girls and young women aged 15–19 years.<sup>33</sup>

### Children born to the youngest and oldest mothers face the highest risk of dying before age <span class="number-literal">5</span>

### Figure <span class="number-literal">15</span>. Under-f﻿ii ve mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by mother’s age (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: The under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates by mother’s age are derived from UNICEF analysis based on DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources for `r note_number(length(note_country_sets$motherage$U5MR), "64", "note-fig15-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` countries.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">40</span> {#pdf-page-40 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

Children born to adolescent mothers and to women older than 40 face higher mortality rates throughout the first five years of life (see Figure 15). Though the risks are highest among children born to the oldest mothers, these deaths constitute only around `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '40-49', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0230")` per cent of under-five deaths, compared to the much higher proportion (approximately `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '<20', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0231")` per cent) of deaths among children born to adolescent mothers (see Figure 16).

The under-five mortality rate for children of adolescent mothers was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '<20', '20-29'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0232")` times as high as that of children born to mothers aged 20–29 years, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '<20', '20-29'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0233")` deaths per 1,000 live births. Meanwhile, for children born to mothers aged 40–49 years, the risk of dying before age 5 was `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '40-49', '20-29'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0234")` times that of children born to mothers aged 20–29 years, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '40-49', '20-29'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0235")` deaths per 1,000 live births.

These trends remain more or less the same across the first five years of life, with little variation between newborns and children aged 1–59 months.

### Adolescent mothers shoulder the greatest relative burden of under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths

### Figure <span class="number-literal">16</span>. Percentage of live births, under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths, neonatal deaths and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months deaths, by mother’s age (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Children born to adolescent mothers account for a slightly higher percentage of under-five and neonatal deaths than their share of live births. While `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '<20', 'wgt.birth'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0236")` per cent of live births took place among mothers younger than 20 years old, `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '<20', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0237")` per cent of all under-five deaths and `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'NMR', '<20', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0238")` per cent of neonatal deaths occurred in this group. Only `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '40-49', 'wgt.birth'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0239")` per cent of live births occurred among women above age 40, and their share of under-five deaths was around `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '40-49', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0240")` per cent. More than half (`r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '20-29', 'wgt.birth'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0241")` per cent) of children were born to mothers aged 20–29 years, with that age group experiencing roughly half of all under-five deaths.

### Mother’s age remains an important factor

Under-five mortality rates by mother’s age have declined for all age groups since 2000 in `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_country_count('motherage'), digits = 0, evidence = "trend_summary_nc_2000_2024_PD.csv"), "code-number-0242")` countries with trend data. With similar rates of progress for the different maternal age categories, the absolute gap narrowed while relative disparities remained at similar levels. The risk of children born to adolescent mothers compared to children born to mothers aged 20–29 years has remained steady at `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio("Mother's age", 'U5MR', '<20', '20-29'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0243")`.

For neonates and children aged 1–59 months, the ratio followed similar patterns.

## Birth interval: What if I’m born within <span class="number-literal">two</span> years of a sibling?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">43</span> {#pdf-page-43 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

As birth intervals shorten (i.e., as the period of time since the previous birth decreases), the odds that a child will die before turning 5 increase. The link between birth interval and child mortality reiterates the need for widespread access to family planning services and education that ensure mothers understand optimal birth spacing for their own and their children’s survival – particularly among groups of women likely to have a higher number of births.<sup>34, 35, 36, 37, 38</sup> This connection can be largely attributed to differences in the background characteristics of mothers with high fertility versus low fertility.<sup>39</sup>

In sub-Saharan Africa, nearly one in two births occur at short birth intervals (i.e., less than two years apart).<sup>40</sup>

### Longer intervals between births increase the odds of survival to age <span class="number-literal">5</span>

### Figure <span class="number-literal">18</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by birth interval (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: The under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates by birth interval are derived from UNICEF analysis based on DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources for `r note_number(length(note_country_sets$birthinterval$U5MR), "69", "note-fig18-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` countries.

The under-five mortality rate for children born within two years of a sibling was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '<2', '3'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0258")` times that of children born with a birth interval of three years, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '<2', '3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0259")` deaths per 1,000 live births (see Figure 18). The odds of survival improve as birth intervals lengthen, most notably when births are spaced at three-year intervals: The under-five mortality rate drops from `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '<2'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0260")` deaths per 1,000 live births for birth intervals of less than two years to `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '2'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0261")` deaths per 1,000 live births for birth intervals of two years, to `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0262")` deaths per 1,000 live births

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">44</span> {#pdf-page-44 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

for three-year intervals and further declines to `r code_number_display(calc_black(weighted_rate('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '>=4'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0263")` deaths per 1,000 live births for intervals of four years or more. These findings underscore the World Health Organization recommendations to wait a minimum of 24 months following a live birth to attempt the next pregnancy.<sup>41</sup>

Among both neonates and 1–59-month-olds, children born within two years of a sibling face the highest mortality risks. Short birth intervals are a particularly substantial risk factor in the first month of life: The neonatal mortality rate for children with a birth interval of less than two years was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Birth interval', 'NMR', '<2', '3'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0264")` times that of those with a birth interval of three years, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth interval', 'NMR', '<2', '3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0265")` deaths per 1,000 live births. The 1–59-months mortality rate for children with a birth interval of less than two years was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Birth interval', 'MR1t59', '<2', '3'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0266")` times that of children with a birth interval of three years, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth interval', 'MR1t59', '<2', '3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0267")` deaths per 1,000 children aged 28 days.

### Mothers who give birth to children within <span class="number-literal">two</span>-year intervals experience an unequal share of under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths

### Figure <span class="number-literal">19</span>. Percentage of live births, under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths, neonatal deaths and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months deaths by birth interval (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

More than two thirds of the burden of under-five deaths is carried by women who give birth either within or at the two-year mark of a prior birth. The greatest relative burden is seen in the shortest birth interval (under two years): `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '<2', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0268")` per cent of all under-five deaths, `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth interval', 'NMR', '<2', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0269")` per cent of neonatal deaths and `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth interval', 'MR1t59', '<2', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0270")` per cent of deaths among children aged 1–59 months occurred in this category, compared to `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth interval', 'U5MR', '<2', 'wgt.birth'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0271")` per cent of live births (see Figure 19).

## Short birth intervals continue to be a risk factor

Since 2000, the mortality risk for children with birth intervals of less than two years has continued to be more than twice that of children spaced three years or more apart. The disparity ratio increased from `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_ratio('birthinterval', '<2', '3', 'U5MR', 2000), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregates_2000_2024_from_extrapolation_benchmarked.xlsx"), "code-number-0272")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_ratio('birthinterval', '<2', '3', 'U5MR', 2024), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregates_2000_2024_from_extrapolation_benchmarked.xlsx"), "code-number-0273")` based on aggregate trend data for `r note_number(trend_country_counts$birthinterval, "50", "code-number-0274", "country_projection_2000_2024_from_extrapolation_benchmarked.xlsx; distinct Country.Code with complete group/year coverage")` countries, although the absolute differences between birth intervals declined. Overall trends, however, indicate that more women are spacing births at greater intervals while having less children.

**CRITICAL FOCUS**

## What role does a child’s sex play in shaping under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rates?

Sex differences in mortality are an important area of research when examining equity in health outcomes. Due to biological factors, under-five mortality rates among males are expected to be higher, on average, than among females. For instance, the estimated global under-five mortality rate for girls in 2024 was `r code_number_display(calc_black(world_female_u5mr_2024, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Region_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0296")` deaths per 1,000 live births, while the rate for boys was `r code_number_display(calc_black(world_male_u5mr_2024, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Region_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0297")` deaths per 1,000 live births (see Figure 21).<sup>42</sup> In some countries, however, mortality rates for girls are significantly higher than what would be expected based on global patterns of sex ratios (i.e., male/female mortality, where any value above 1 indicates boys face higher risks of death than girls and values below 1 indicate girls face the greater risk).<sup>43</sup> Notably, the number of countries showing higher-than-expected mortality for girls has fallen from `r code_number_display(calc_black(girls_higher_1990, digits = 0, evidence = "table.female.df.csv"), "code-number-0298")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(girls_higher_2024, digits = 0, evidence = "table.female.df.csv"), "code-number-0299")` since 1990, with the remaining countries primarily located in Central and Southern Asia.

The Central and Southern Asia region has some of the world’s lowest sex ratios for under-five mortality, infant mortality (children aged &lt;1 year) and child mortality (children aged 1–4 years). Across these three indicators, a sex ratio below 1 – indicating higher female mortality – was observed in only one indicator from 2000 to 2024: Central and Southern Asia’s child mortality rate. No estimates were available for neonates.

Globally and across most regions, however, sex ratios tend to increase as mortality decreases (see Figure 21). Sex ratios are higher among infants than among children aged 1–4 years, suggesting infant boys are more likely to die than infant girls, whereas girls face greater relative risks between the ages of 1 and 4. In the regions of Australia and New Zealand and Europe and Northern America, however – where mortality levels are relatively low – sex ratios have decreased over the last two decades and male mortality risks among the 1–4-years age group are greater than among male infants.

What is driving these divergent outcomes by country and region? They may be tied to sex-dependent allocation in certain environments when it comes to resources like nutrition and access to health care, both of which are critical to fighting infectious diseases associated with death among children aged 1–4 years. Examining the age-specific causes of death and any sex differentials in resource allocation that may drive sex differences in mortality is thus an important component to reducing preventable mortality overall.

## Birth order: What if I’m the <span class="number-literal">fourth</span>-born or later child in my family?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">50</span> {#pdf-page-50 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

Whether a child celebrates their fifth birthday or not can depend on their birth order and whether they are firstborn or joining many siblings. Child mortality is significantly associated with birth order – with fourth- or later-born children facing the highest risks.<sup>44, 45</sup>

While the global fertility rate has declined by about half since 1950 – reaching `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(external_value("fertility_global_2024"), 1), digits = 1, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0300")` children per woman in 2024 – fertility rates continue to be much higher in sub-Saharan Africa, at about `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(external_value("fertility_ssa_2024"), 1), digits = 1, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0301")` children per woman.<sup>46</sup>

### <span class="number-literal">Fourth</span>- or later-born children are the most likely to die in the <span class="number-literal">first</span> <span class="number-literal">five</span> years of life

### Figure <span class="number-literal">22</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by birth order (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: The under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates by birth order are derived from UNICEF analysis based on DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources for `r note_number(length(note_country_sets$birthorder$U5MR), "69", "note-fig22-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` countries.

If a child is the fourth or greater addition to a family, they face an under-five mortality risk that is `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Birth order', 'U5MR', '4+', '2-3'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0302")` times that of a child born second or third, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth order', 'U5MR', '4+', '2-3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0303")` deaths per 1,000 live births. Firstborn children have a slightly higher neonatal mortality risk than second- or third-born children (see Figure 22). In the first month of life, the risk of dying for fourth- or higher-born children is `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Birth order', 'NMR', '4+', '2-3'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0304")` times as high as the risk faced by second- or third-born children, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth order', 'NMR', '4+', '2-3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0305")` deaths per 1,000 live births. As they mature to age 5, these chances of survival do not improve: The 1–59-months mortality rate for children joining three or more siblings in a family was on average `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_ratio('Birth order', 'MR1t59', '4+', '2-3'), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0306")` times that of the second- or third-born children, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth order', 'MR1t59', '4+', '2-3'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0307")` deaths per 1,000 children aged 28 days.

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">51</span> {#pdf-page-51 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### Children who are born <span class="number-literal">fourth</span> or later bear an unequal burden of death before age <span class="number-literal">5</span>

### Figure <span class="number-literal">23</span>. Percentage of live births, under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> deaths, neonatal deaths and deaths among children aged <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span> months, by birth order (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Children of higher birth order account for a higher share of under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months deaths than their share of live births (see Figure 23). While `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth order', 'U5MR', '4+', 'wgt.birth'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0308")` per cent of live births were of children born fourth or later, this group accounted for `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth order', 'U5MR', '4+', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0309")` per cent of all under-five deaths. This percentage increases with age: `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth order', 'NMR', '4+', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0310")` per cent of neonatal deaths took place among children born fourth or later, compared to `r code_number_display(calc_black(group_share('Birth order', 'MR1t59', '4+', 'wgt.death'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0311")` per cent of deaths among children aged 1–59 months.

## High birth order remains a risk factor

Under-five mortality rates have declined for all children regardless of their birth order since 2000, based on `r note_number(trend_country_counts$birthorder, "50", "code-number-0312", "country_projection_2000_2024_from_extrapolation_benchmarked.xlsx; distinct Country.Code with complete group/year coverage")` countries with trend data. While absolute differences declined, relative differences increased slightly over time: fourth- or higher-born children now have an under-five mortality rate `r code_number_display(calc_red(birth_order_aggregate_ratio, digits = 1, suffix = " times as high", evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0313")` as second- or third-born children, compared to `r code_number_display(calc_black(trend_ratio('birthorder', '4+_', '2-3_', 'U5MR', 2000), digits = 1, evidence = "aggregates_2000_2024_from_extrapolation_benchmarked.xlsx"), "code-number-0314")` in 2000.

Birth order was grouped into first birth, second and third birth, and fourth and higher birth for each recorded birth. These groupings are child-specific and not simply based on the number of times the mother has given birth to a child (parity) at the time of the interview.

## Interacting maternal fertility-related conditions

This analysis captures the inherent risks and benefits associated with pregnancy during different times in a woman’s life and the need to inform women accordingly. Many of the conditions described in this report are intertwined: Birth spacing, maternal age at birth and birth order are closely related and have joint impact on child mortality.<sup>47</sup> Mortality risks due to short birth intervals may be determined by maternal age, age at pregnancy, number of children, socio-economic status and/or death of a previous child.<sup>48</sup> Mortality risks associated with firstborn children may also be a factor of maternal age. The risks associated with high birth order and advanced maternal age could relate to maternal nutritional depletion, less care-seeking with multiple children, infection transmission from siblings, and the division of resources between siblings.

The association between maternal fertility-related conditions and child mortality outcomes was analysed in order to provide insight into how these factors interact, using data from the latest `r note_number(fertility_surveys, "150", "note-p53-fertility-surveys", "fertility/dhs database.csv and mics database.csv; distinct survey samples and row counts", digits = 0)` Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) and Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), which covered `r code_number_display(calc_black(fertility_births / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "fertility DHS and MICS microdata"), "code-number-0327")` million births. The analysis found that facing a double fertility risk – such as a birth interval of less than two years and being born fourth or higher – increases the likelihood of a child dying before age 5 by over `r code_number_display(calc_black(floor(100 * (fertility_double_rr - 1) / 10) * 10, digits = 0, evidence = "fertility interaction result.xlsx"), "code-number-0328")` per cent compared to children born at longer intervals and lower-

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">54</span> {#pdf-page-54 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

order births. Children born with two or three fertility-related risk factors have a higher mortality risk compared to children with one risk factor or no risk factor. For children with two risk factors, the largest risks are observed for short birth spacing and the youngest and oldest mothers. For children born to the oldest mothers, with a high birth order and at short birth intervals, the risk of dying before age 5 is relatively higher compared to children with one single risk or no risks (see Figure `r calc_black(report_figures$fertility_interaction, digits = 0, evidence = "calculated report structure")`).

### Figure <span class="number-literal">25</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality, neonatal mortality and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality risks by maternal fertility-related conditions

Note: UNICEF analysis based on dataset from `r note_number(fertility_surveys, "150", "note-fig25-surveys", "fertility/dhs database.csv and mics database.csv; distinct survey samples and row counts", digits = 0)` surveys, including a combined total of `r note_number(fertility_births / 1e6, "8.2", "note-fig25-births", "fertility/dhs database.csv and mics database.csv; distinct survey samples and row counts", digits = 1)` million births. The reference categories for the single risk factors are: 1) Birth order: Second and third births; 2) Mother’s age: 20–29 years; and 3) Birth interval: Previous birth three years ago. For double and triple risk factors, the reference category combines the reference categories of the single risk factors. For example, the reference category for previous birth less than two years and fourth or higher-order birth is the combination of previous birth three years ago and second or third birth. The relative risk of each double risk factor is compared to the reference category’s mortality risk.

**CRITICAL FOCUS**

## Stillbirth and inequities

The stillbirth rate is an important indicator of the quality of care received during pregnancy and childbirth. According to the latest available estimates on late gestation stillbirths (i.e., stillbirths that occur during the third trimester of pregnancy), an estimated `r code_number_display(calc_black(stillbirth_2023 / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0330")` million babies were stillborn in 2023 – the equivalent of one stillbirth every `r code_number_display(calc_black(seconds_per_year / stillbirth_2023, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0331")` seconds.<sup>49</sup> And between 2000 and 2023, approximately `r code_number_display(calc_black(stillbirth_2000_2023 / 1e6, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0332")` million babies were stillborn. These sobering figures exclude stillbirths at earlier gestational stages and are likely underestimates, as many countries do not systematically record or report these deaths and stillbirths are largely missing from worldwide data tracking systems.

The burden of stillbirths is unjustly carried by pregnant women in two regions – sub-Saharan Africa and Southern Asia – where 8 in 10 (`r code_number_display(calc_black(stillbirth_regions_share, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0333")` per cent) of these deaths took place in 2023.

Like under-five deaths, most stillbirths are preventable, as the key causes of stillbirth – maternal infections, non-communicable diseases, nutrition and lifestyle factors – are largely treatable. Many of the risk factors linked to higher rates of under-five mortality in this report – like household wealth, maternal level of education and place of residence – have also been associated with a higher risk of stillbirth (see Figure 26). Evidence suggests that these disparities are part of a broader pattern of structural inequality in stillbirth risk observed across health systems and regions, regardless of income level.<sup>50, 51</sup>

- In low- and middle-income countries, mothers who experienced a stillbirth were more likely to be from the poorest households, have low levels of education<sup> </sup>and live in rural areas.<sup> </sup><sup>52,</sup> <sup>53, 54</sup> Similar outcomes have also been observed in high-income settings – including contexts where universal health coverage is available.<sup>55</sup>

- Adolescent mothers and those older than 35 experience higher rates of stillbirth.<sup>56, 57</sup>

- Higher stillbirth rates have been recorded among different ethnic groups in high-income countries, pointing to social and structural determinants of risk that intersect and extend beyond income.<sup>58</sup>

- Birth interval, birth order and birth size have also been associated with a heightened risk of stillbirth.

Among the `r code_number_display(calc_black(length(unique(stillbirth_country$ISO3Code)), digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0334")` countries for which the UN IGME stillbirth estimates are generated, `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(stillbirth_no_data, digits = -1), digits = 0, evidence = "data_for_plotting_2025-03-10.xlsx"), "code-number-0335")` countries have no stillbirth data, and an additional `r code_number_display(calc_black(round(stillbirth_without_quality_data, digits = -1), digits = 0, evidence = "data_for_plotting_2025-03-10.xlsx"), "code-number-0336")` countries lack quality stillbirth data. Many of the countries with the greatest data gaps are also those bearing the largest burden of stillbirths. The inequities in child mortality rates described in this report illustrate the need to improve the data on stillbirths, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, so that efforts to prevent stillbirths are

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">56</span> {#pdf-page-56 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

not only equitably distributed among all women, but also so that those facing the highest risks are identified and reached.

Surveys that include full pregnancy histories (as opposed to full birth histories) offer great potential to close many of these data gaps, as they count and capture every birth – whether a live birth or stillbirth.<sup>59, 60</sup> They would also allow for more nuanced assessment of disparities in stillbirths related to the socio-economic factors and maternal fertility-related conditions described in this report.

Stillbirths must be included in burden assessments and relevant indicators, and efforts designed to address inequities in under-five mortality must also institute measures that prevent stillbirths.

### Figure <span class="number-literal">26</span>. Stillbirth rates by household wealth, mother’s education, residence, mother’s age and birth interval (<span class="number-literal">2023</span>)

Note: The analysis is based on `r code_number_display(calc_black(stillbirth_dhs_survey_count, digits = 0, evidence = "DHS_API_download_2025-02-18.csv"), "code-number-0337")` DHS surveys conducted between `r code_number_display(calc_black(as.character(stillbirth_dhs_year_start), evidence = "DHS_API_download_2025-02-18.csv"), "code-number-0338")` and `r code_number_display(calc_black(as.character(stillbirth_dhs_year_end), evidence = "DHS_API_download_2025-02-18.csv"), "code-number-0339")` in `r code_number_display(calc_black(stillbirth_dhs_country_count, digits = 0, evidence = "DHS_API_download_2025-02-18.csv"), "code-number-0340")` low- and middle-income countries that accounted for `r code_number_display(calc_black(100 * stillbirth_dhs_share, digits = 0, evidence = "DHS_API_download_2025-02-18.csv and UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0341")` per cent (`r note_number(note_stillbirth_deaths / 1e6, "1.5", "note-fig26-stillbirths", "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv; DHS_API_download_2025-02-18.csv; selected country sum", digits = 1)` million) of global stillbirths in `r calc_black(as.character(stillbirth_estimate_year), evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv")`. Rates were computed by aggregating stillbirths and births across surveys. After calculating the number of stillbirths and total births in each equity group, the distribution of births by equity group in the surveys was applied to the live birth figures from World Population Prospects `r calc_black(as.character(wpp_live_birth_vintage), evidence = "World Population Prospects 2024")` and UN IGME stillbirth figures for `r calc_black(as.character(stillbirth_estimate_year), evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv")` to calculate the aggregated stillbirth rate in each group.

## Birth size: What if I’m a small newborn?

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">58</span> {#pdf-page-58 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### KEY FACT

Smaller birth size is strongly linked to a higher risk of neonatal mortality, and most deaths during the first 28 days of life are attributable to being born preterm, small for gestational age or with low birthweight. When they do survive to age 5, small and vulnerable newborns are also at risk of facing long-term health issues as they mature.<sup>61, 62</sup> Mothers of small and vulnerable newborns may suffer from undernutrition, infections and environmental exposure.<sup>63</sup> These conditions are also linked to stillbirths, `r code_number_display(calc_black(stillbirth_2023 / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME_SBR_CountryResults.csv"), "code-number-0345")` million of which occur annually (see p. 55).

This risk factor underscores the importance of targeting interventions to improve fetal growth and address the determinants of low birthweight, such as maternal health and nutrition.

In 2020, `r code_number_display(calc_black(external_value("small_vulnerable_newborns_2020_millions"), digits = 1, evidence = "external_verified_claims.csv"), "code-number-0346")` million newborns were considered to be small and vulnerable – or one in four babies worldwide.<sup>64</sup>

### Babies who are small or very small are more likely to die during the <span class="number-literal">first</span> month of life than larger babies

### Figure <span class="number-literal">27</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate, neonatal mortality rate and <span class="number-literal">1</span>–<span class="number-literal">59</span>-months mortality rate, by birth size (<span class="number-literal">2024</span>)

Note: The under-five, neonatal and 1–59-months mortality rates by birth size are derived from UNICEF analysis based on DHS, MICS and other nationally representative sources. `r note_birth_size_comparability`: The under-five mortality rate aggregate is based on `r note_number(note_birth_size_counts[["U5MR"]], "7", "note-fig27-u5-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` countries, neonatal mortality rate on `r note_number(note_birth_size_counts[["NMR"]], "40", "note-fig27-nmr-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; aggregate_dimension_codes()", digits = 0)` countries, and 1–59-months mortality rate on `r note_number(note_birth_size_counts[["MR1t59"]], "7", "note-fig27-mr1t59-countries", "deaths-and-births-country_2026-06-23.csv; matching birth-size U5MR/NMR contributors; 02_produce-aggregate.R section 11", digits = 0)` countries.

Birth size is an important factor for newborn survival. The neonatal mortality rate for very small or small newborns is almost twice that of newborns with average or large size, with an absolute difference of `r code_number_display(calc_black(aggregate_rate_difference('Birth size', 'NMR', 'small.vsmall', 'av.large'), digits = 0, evidence = "aggregate_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0347")` deaths per 1,000 live births.

Children of small or very small size account for a higher percentage of neonatal deaths compared to their share of live births. ## Disparity ratios and birth size: How pronounced are inequities between different groups of children within countries?

### Figure <span class="number-literal">29</span>. Neonatal mortality rates by small and average birth size in selected countries

Across the `r code_number_display(calc_black(nrow(birth_size_nmr_detail), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0350")` countries studied, the neonatal mortality rate disparity ratio between very small or small newborns and average or large newborns ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(birth_size_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0351")` in Ethiopia to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(birth_size_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0352")` in Cambodia (see Figure `r calc_black(report_figures$birth_size_country, digits = 0, evidence = "calculated report structure")`). In half of the countries, the risk of dying before turning 1 month for very small or small newborns was `r code_number_display(calc_black(median(birth_size_nmr_detail$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0354")` times higher than it was among average or large newborns. For older children under 5 years of age, the disparity ratio ranged from `r code_number_display(calc_black(min(birth_size_u5$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0355")` to `r code_number_display(calc_black(max(birth_size_u5$ratio), digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0356")` among the very few countries with data.

### BEHIND THE DATA: ESTIMATING CHILD MORTALITY AND BIRTH SIZE

### Map <span class="number-literal">8</span>. Countries with available survey or sample vital registration data for newborn birth size analysis

Note: This map does not reflect a position by UNICEF on the legal status of any country or territory or the delimitation of any frontiers.

The analysis of mortality by birth size is based on data for neonates from `r code_number_display(calc_black(nrow(birth_size_nmr_detail), digits = 0, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0357")` countries, which accounted for `r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_birthsize$nmr_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0358")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_birthsize$nmr_deaths / 1e6, digits = 1, evidence = "UNIGME2025_Country_Rates_&_Deaths.csv"), "code-number-0359")` million) of global neonatal deaths and `r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_birthsize$birth_percent, digits = 0, evidence = "data_livebirths.csv"), "code-number-0360")` per cent (`r code_number_display(calc_black(coverage_birthsize$births / 1e6, digits = 0, evidence = "data_livebirths.csv"), "code-number-0361")` million) of live births in 2024. Reliable data with sufficient cases were more often available for neonates than for older children under age 5. If the denominator was too small for the calculation of the mortality rate, the estimate was not published.

Given the small number of surveys and cases, estimates of mortality by birth size used published values with 10-year reference intervals and did not recalculate them using the shorter reference period of 5 years that was used for the other indicators.

The mother’s estimate of the baby’s size at birth was used, with categories of very small, smaller than average, and average or larger.

**CRITICAL FOCUS**

## Subnational trends in under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality

The SDG agenda commits to leaving no one behind. As this publication highlights, realizing that goal in child mortality demands a focus on those children who continue to face disproportionately greater threats to their survival.

While national-level estimates are critical to tracking progress towards achieving the SDG targets on under-five mortality, they can also obscure uneven subnational trends within countries – which, if left unaddressed, threaten to leave the children facing the greatest mortality risks behind.<sup>65</sup> When national-level estimates are broken down by administrative level – e.g., municipalities, districts, provinces, states – inequities between different groups of children emerge, even in countries where under-five mortality rates are relatively low and/or SDG targets have already been met.

### Applying a local-level lens to country estimates reveals vastly different chances of survival for children in low- and lower-middle-income countries

### Map <span class="number-literal">9</span>. Under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rate at administrative levels <span class="number-literal">1</span> and <span class="number-literal">2</span> (<span class="number-literal">2021</span>)

Note: This map does not reflect a position by UNICEF on the legal status of any country or territory or the delimitation of any frontiers.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">62</span> {#pdf-page-62 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

Current mortality levels, progress in reducing under-five mortality and distance to SDG mortality targets are highly varied when examined at subnational level. In Nigeria, for instance, where the national under-five mortality rate for 2021 was `r code_number_display(calc_black(nigeria_national_u5mr_2021, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2022_Country_Rates.csv"), "code-number-0362")` deaths per 1,000 live births, rates at administrative level 1 ranged from a low of `r code_number_display(calc_black(nigeria_subnational_u5mr_2021[['min']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0363")` deaths per 1,000 live births to a high of `r code_number_display(calc_black(nigeria_subnational_u5mr_2021[['max']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0364")` deaths per 1,000 live births – a fivefold difference (see Map 9). In Angola, the national neonatal mortality rate was `r code_number_display(calc_black(angola_national_nmr_2021, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2022_Country_Rates.csv"), "code-number-0365")` deaths per 1,000 live births in 2021, while subnational rates at administrative level 2 ranged from a low of `r code_number_display(calc_black(angola_subnational_nmr_2021[['min']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0366")` deaths per 1,000 live births to a high of `r code_number_display(calc_black(angola_subnational_nmr_2021[['max']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0367")` deaths per 1,000 live births.

Looking at reductions in mortality rates, progress by locality has also been uneven, as seen in Haiti: Its national neonatal mortality rate has declined by `r code_number_display(calc_black(haiti_national_nmr_decline, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2022_Country_Rates.csv"), "code-number-0368")` per cent since 2000, but the percentage decline within administrative level 1 divisions ranged from a high of `r code_number_display(calc_black(haiti_subnational_nmr_decline[['max']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0369")` per cent (almost twice the national average) to a low of just `r code_number_display(calc_black(haiti_subnational_nmr_decline[['min']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0370")` per cent (a mere third of national progress) (see Figure `r calc_black(report_figures$subnational_decline, digits = 0, evidence = "calculated report structure")`). In Chad, the national under-five mortality rate has declined by `r code_number_display(calc_black(chad_national_u5mr_decline, digits = 0, evidence = "UNIGME2022_Country_Rates.csv"), "code-number-0372")` per cent since 2000, while the percentage decline within administrative level 1 ranged from a low of `r code_number_display(calc_black(chad_subnational_u5mr_decline[['min']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0373")` per cent (i.e., an increase) to a high of `r code_number_display(calc_black(chad_subnational_u5mr_decline[['max']], digits = 0, evidence = "Subnational_estimates_2023-08-15.xlsx"), "code-number-0374")` per cent.

## Subnational disparities in under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality exist in wealthier countries

### Map `r calc_black(page64_map_number, digits = 0, evidence = "calculated report structure")`. Subnational under-<span class="number-literal">five</span> mortality rates at administrative level `r calc_black(page64_admin_level, digits = 0, evidence = "subnational database_eurostat.xlsx: NUTS1 selection")` for selected upper-middle- and high-income countries (`r code_number_display(calc_black(as.character(page64_year_min), evidence = "subnational database_supplementary.xlsx; subnational database_eurostat.xlsx"), "code-number-0385")`-`r code_number_display(calc_black(as.character(page64_year_max), evidence = "subnational database_supplementary.xlsx; subnational database_eurostat.xlsx"), "code-number-0386")`)

Note: Rates are based on unrounded numbers; value ranges are greater than the lower bound number and less than or equal to the upper bound number. This map does not reflect a position by UNICEF on the legal status of any country or territory or the delimitation of any frontiers.

As of `r code_number_display(calc_black(as.character(page64_china_year), evidence = "subnational database_supplementary.xlsx: China reference year; PDF page 64 annotation"), "code-number-0389")`, `r code_number_display(calc_black(page64_china_above_target, digits = 0, evidence = "subnational database_supplementary.xlsx"), "code-number-0390")` out of `r code_number_display(calc_black(page64_china_region_count, digits = 0, evidence = "subnational database_supplementary.xlsx"), "code-number-0391")` subnational regions in China had not met the target. ## Evidence for every child

The interventions to reduce under-five mortality are well established. When women and children have access to quality care before and during pregnancy and childbirth – including sexual and reproductive health services, care for small and sick newborns, routine immunization and adequate nutrition – more children will survive and thrive.

Yet this report highlights a persistent reality: These preventative measures remain unevenly accessible based on the conditions into which a child is born, leaving families around the world to continue to unnecessarily experience the loss of children. While the data explored in this analysis offer important insights into these patterns of inequity, they do not capture the full picture. Better data and evidence are also needed to understand how additional dimensions – such as ethnicity, disability status, migration status and exposure to conflict – influence child survival.

In this way, an equity-driven approach to data collection, analysis and use plays an instrumental role in helping countries focus attention and resources where they are most likely to have the greatest impact on child mortality. Viewing under-five mortality rates through an equity lens enables countries to look beyond national averages to identify the children most at risk of dying before age 5 and the barriers that place them at risk.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">67</span> {#pdf-page-67 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

An equity-focused analysis can answer critical questions such as:

### Which children are being left behind?

Which groups of children are most likely to die before age 5 when mortality is viewed through the lens of wealth, maternal education, place of residence and birth characteristics? Which age groups – newborns? children aged 1–59 months? – are most vulnerable?

### Where would targeted investments most substantially improve child survival?

Which geographic areas – rural communities? specific regions or districts? fragile and conflict-affected settings? – are home to the children facing the greatest risk of dying before age 5?

### Which barriers are shaping chances of survival?

What do patterns in under-five mortality tell us about underlying barriers such as financial constraints, limited access to maternal and newborn care, gaps in adolescent health services, or insufficient birth spacing and family planning support?

### Who is being missed – even when national targets are met?

In countries that have achieved SDG targets for child mortality, which population groups continue to experience elevated risks that are masked by national averages?

Together, these questions provide a road map for action – showing who is being left behind, where the greatest mortality burdens persist and how resources can be targeted most effectively.

Reducing under-five mortality requires more than sustaining progress at the national level. It requires the deliberate and strategic use of evidence to guide action equitably – ensuring that resources and services are directed towards the populations facing the greatest barriers to survival. This includes:

Strengthening access to maternal, newborn and childcare where mortality remains highest, alongside reproductive health services and education Implementing interventions that focus on underserved populations, paying close attention to geographic inequities in rural areas and/or at subnational level Addressing the social and economic barriers linked to greater mortality risks (e.g., poverty, education) Investing in data systems so that they can capture inequities, track progress among

vulnerable groups and hold governments accountable Every child, regardless of where they are born, their socio-economic status, gender, ethnicity or circumstance, deserves an equal opportunity to survive and reach their full potential. Urgent, evidence-based action and targeted investments are needed to address the root causes of disadvantage and ensure that those furthest behind are reached first. By prioritizing equity today, countries can accelerate progress towards the SDGs and take one step closer to a world in which every child has a fair chance to survive and thrive.

## Annex

## Measures used in this analysis

This publication presents relative disparity ratios to compare gaps in mortality rates between two distinct groups and absolute differences to measure how wide those gaps are. Both measures are useful for understanding inequality as they offer different insights – for instance, relative disparity ratios can remain the same over time while absolute gaps can decline or increase.

Other statistical measures to assess inequality across groups – such as the slope index, between-group variance, concentration index and Theil index – can also be used. The Theil index was used in this analysis to examine ethnic groups in order to provide a relative measure of inequality across more than two groups and take group size into account. Absolute inequalities can also be measured with the slope index and between-group variance, while also taking group size into account; they were not, however, used in the findings presented here.

These summary indices often complement each other and offer a more complete picture of inequalities, thus helping us understand vulnerabilities. For instance, a disparity ratio might be relatively small between two groups (indicating little inequality), but once population weight is accounted for in calculating the Theil index, a higher degree of inequity may be discovered. While the other measures described above can enhance statistical analysis, they can also make interpretation more complex. Given the correlation of different relative and absolute measures, the findings in this analysis use interpretable disparity ratios and absolute differences as much as possible.

The correlation and country ranking across measures is high within absolute and relative measures of under-five mortality rates by wealth quintiles and other equity dimensions when group sizes are similar. For instance, the correlation between the concentration index and the disparity ratio by wealth quintile for under-five mortality rates is `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_concentration_disparity_correlation, digits = 2, evidence = "inequality_indices.csv"), "code-number-0420")` (see Figure `r calc_black(report_figures$inequality_measures, digits = 0, evidence = "calculated report structure")`). The correlation and country ranking across absolute and relative measures of under-five mortality rate by wealth quintile is weak since relative inequalities can be very different from absolute inequalities.

<!-- PDF page -->

#### Source PDF page <span class="number-literal">69</span> {#pdf-page-69 .unnumbered .unlisted .pdf-page}

### What do disparity ratios tell us about child mortality and inequities?

The disparity ratio is derived by dividing the highest numerical value by the lowest numerical value – in this case using mortality rates associated with the lowest or highest levels of mother’s education or wealth, for instance. The greater the resulting ratio’s numerical value, the greater the inequalities between groups are. A disparity ratio of `r calc_black(equal_ratio, digits = 0, evidence = "ratio definition")` indicates that the risk of dying by age 5 is the same between groups measured. Increasing disparity ratios over time indicate widening disparities between under-five mortality rates, while declining disparity ratios demonstrate the relative risks are leveling out.

A lower ratio does not indicate absolute levels themselves are higher or lower. For instance, the disparity ratio in child mortality by wealth quintile in South Sudan is low, at `r code_number_display(calc_black(wealth_u5$ratio[wealth_u5$Country.Name == 'South Sudan'], digits = 1, evidence = "country-specific-database-cleaned-igme-wealth_2026-06-23.csv"), "code-number-0423")`, but this is because the country’s child mortality rates – which are among the world’s highest – are roughly the same across wealth quintiles.

### How can disparity ratios be used to inform programming?

Zooming in on Southern Asia as an example – where neonatal mortality rates remain stubbornly high – disparities in mortality rates by mother’s education level in Nepal are notable, at `r code_number_display(calc_black(nepal_education_ratio, digits = 1, evidence = "riskfactors-data-CMEinfo.csv (in_aggregate = TRUE)"), "code-number-0424")`, comparing children born by mothers without education to children born by mothers with secondary education or higher. This indicates the importance of prioritizing girls’ education and targeting interventions among mothers with the lowest levels of education in order to successfully and meaningfully reduce the country’s overall neonatal mortality rate.
